hy4-preview/06-product-planning/RESPONSE.md

RESPONSE — The three riskiest assumptions

These are the three assumptions in PLAN.md §2 that, if wrong, are most likely to invalidate the design rather than merely delay it. Each is listed with what breaks, what in the plan would change, and how to close it before implementation starts.

1. The 24-hour purge and the audit history can be satisfied simultaneously (A9 + A10)

The assumption. "Accepted" is a server-side status transition, the 24-hour clock starts at the server's acceptance timestamp, and the regulatory audit history can be retained after local customer PII is removed — because the retained audit entries can be pseudonymous (hashes and opaque refs instead of names and addresses).

Why it is the riskiest. The brief states two requirements that pull in opposite directions: keep an audit history, and delete customer data within 24 hours. If the audit history is legally required to record who signed and what was recorded, then the very fields that make the audit meaningful are the fields we must delete. There is no engineering trick that resolves this — it is a compliance interpretation, and guessing it wrong produces a regulatory breach that is discovered long after release, on a device that is already in a basement. The secondary risk is the clock: if we key the 24 hours off device time (A13), a skewed clock silently breaches it.

What changes if it is wrong. If identity must be retained locally, the local purge becomes a partial redaction with a compliance-approved retention carve-out, and the device must be treated as in-scope for longer. If instead the purge is absolute, the audit history must be server-side only, and the local audit log can retain nothing but hashes and ids (which is what the plan currently assumes). Either way §8.3 and the audit_log / signatures tables change, and M4's acceptance criteria change with them.

How to close it. Written confirmation from compliance on (a) the start of the clock, (b) the exact enumerated field list that counts as "customer data", and (c) whether the audit entry may reference the signer by hash. Then encoded as a test fixture in M0 — not as a comment in the code.

2. Field-level conflict resolution is safe with per-record integer versions (A7 + A8)

The assumption. The backend team can add a small number of additive sync endpoints — notably a change-log/field-level history — and record versions are bumped on every write path, including web supervisor edits.

Why it is risky. The brief says versions are integers on the record. That tells us that an inspection changed, never which field. Without field-level history, the only available conflict policy is whole-record last-write-wins — which, in an app whose entire purpose is to stop losing inspectors' notes, means the app will systematically discard either the inspector's field notes or the supervisor's correction. That is not a performance problem, it is the original bug reintroduced under a different name. The quieter failure is worse: if even one server write path forgets to bump the version, a client push is accepted as uncontended and overwrites data with no conflict, no signal, no trace.

What changes if it is wrong. If new endpoints are refused, the plan degrades to whole-record LWW with If-Match, conflict resolution UI is reduced to "discard and redo", and D3's recommendation must be escalated to inspection-level check-out as a hard requirement rather than a follow-on. Data loss becomes an expected, documented product trade-off instead of an incident. If versions are reliable but field history is not, we keep the per-op idempotent push but resolve conflicts by full-record comparison and human review on every divergence.

How to close it. Written agreement from backend owners in M0 that the three endpoints in §5.1 are in scope, plus an audit of every server write path for version increments, plus a recurring canary job that flags any record whose version fails to advance while updated_at does.

3. 40 photos per inspection can actually be stored and uploaded in the field (A5 + A6)

The assumption. Worst-case capture is on the order of a few hundred MB per inspection before optimisation, the device has that headroom, and the connection that returns is slow but usable enough to finish the upload.

Why it is risky. This is the assumption that fails in production rather than in review. It combines three unknowns we have not measured: real file sizes on the oldest tablet in the fleet, free storage after weeks of accumulated inspections, and actual throughput at a job site. The failure mode is insidious: the form data is the part we can protect deterministically, but if an inspector finishes an inspection, drives out of the basement, and the 40 photos never finish uploading, from their point of view the inspection is still broken — and they will go back to paper. It also interacts with compliance: photos are customer data and are in scope for the purge, so storage pressure and purge deadlines are competing forces on the same disk.

What changes if it is wrong. If capture volume is larger or storage tighter than assumed, we must reduce resolution at capture, evict uploaded photos aggressively, and make the pre-offline storage projection blocking (§7.9). If upload throughput is worse, chunk sizing, bounded parallelism, and the "optimised by default" policy (D8) all move from optimisation to requirement — and depot-Wi-Fi upload becomes the expected path rather than the fallback. If the legal requirement is original resolution, the entire storage and upload budget must be re-planned, which is exactly why D8 must be answered before M1 rather than discovered at M3.

How to close it. Measure all three numbers in M0: actual captured file size on target hardware, free storage across a sample of in-service devices, and throughput from three representative sites. Then set the chunk size, parallelism, and default quality policy from those measurements — and keep free_storage_bytes, local_db_size_bytes, attachment_upload_success_rate and upload_duration_p95 on the pilot dashboard so the assumptions stay falsifiable after launch.

Common thread

All three share one property: they cannot be closed by writing better code. They are a compliance ruling, a cross-team API commitment, and three field measurements. That is why M0's acceptance criteria are stated as evidence and named owners rather than as completed tasks — the rest of the milestone sequence is only as sound as these three answers.

hy4-preview/06-product-planning/BRIEF.md

Offline inspection brief

Inspectors use company-managed tablets in basements with no signal. Today, a lost connection after opening an inspection can discard notes. They need to open assigned inspections, fill forms, take up to 40 photos, and collect a signature offline. Connectivity may return intermittently. Supervisors can edit the same inspection from the web. Regulations require an audit history and removal of local customer data within 24 hours after an inspection is accepted. Existing server APIs use REST with integer record versions. The mobile app has SQLite but currently treats it as a read-through cache. Product wants a pilot before broad rollout and does not want a full collaborative editor.

hy4-preview/06-product-planning/PLAN.md

Plan 06 — Offline inspection sync

Scope of this document: an engineering plan for making the tablet inspection app usable offline. BRIEF.md is the only product input. Everything not stated there is recorded as an assumption (§2) or an open decision with a recommendation (§16).

1. Problem statement and goal

Inspectors open assigned inspections in basements with no connectivity. Today the local SQLite store is a read-through cache, so a lost connection after opening an inspection can discard notes.

Goal: an inspector can complete an entire assigned inspection — open it, fill the form, capture and annotate up to 40 photos, and collect a signature — with zero network access, and have that work durably reach the server when connectivity returns intermittently, without losing data, without corrupting the regulatory audit history, and without leaving customer data on the device beyond the 24-hour post-acceptance window.

Explicit non-goals (agreed from the brief's "does not want a full collaborative editor"):

  1. No real-time co-editing. There is no live presence, no CRDT, no concurrent in-document collaboration between the tablet and the web.
  2. No peer-to-peer sync between tablets. Devices talk only to the server.
  3. No offline assignment of new inspections to self. The set of inspections available offline is what was synced on the last successful connection.
  4. No offline report generation/PDF export beyond what is already shipped — the completed record syncs, then the server renders.
  5. No offline template authoring or admin functions; supervisors work online.
  6. No rewrite of the existing REST API surface. We add sync endpoints and extend existing ones; we do not replace the API.
  7. No cross-device continuation of a single in-progress inspection (start on this tablet, finish on that one). See D7; recommended as out of scope for the pilot.

2. Assumptions

Each assumption is tagged [load-bearing] if the design would materially change when it is falsified. Validation method is given so these can be closed during M0.

# Assumption Confidence Validation
A1 Inspectors work on company-managed, single-user tablets with a device-level passcode/biometric and MDM available. High Confirm with IT; check MDM capability list
A2 Typical offline window is minutes to a few hours; the same working day, not multiple days. [load-bearing] Medium Instrument time-since-last-sync on current builds; field interviews
A3 A typical inspection is a single inspector; two inspectors do not independently fill the same inspection record concurrently. [load-bearing] Medium Review last quarter of assignment data for co-assignment
A4 The full inventory of assigned inspections for the next working day, plus their form templates and photo capacity, fits in local storage (assumed order of a few hundred records, well under 1 GB). High Measure record + template sizes; measure free disk in fleet
A5 40 photos per inspection at current camera resolution ≈ 200–400 MB worst case per inspection before optimisation. [load-bearing] Medium Measure actual captured file size on target tablet hardware
A6 Upload bandwidth at inspection sites/job trailers is poor but non-zero when connectivity returns (cellular or depot Wi-Fi). Medium Sample throughput from 3 representative sites
A7 The existing REST API can be extended by the backend team within this project; we are not limited to read-only access. [load-bearing] Medium Confirm with backend owners before M1
A8 Server-side record versions are monotonic integers per inspection record, not per field, and are bumped on every mutation including supervisor edits. High (from brief) Read the API/ORM code
A9 "Accepted" is a server-side status transition on the inspection (supervisor accepts), and the 24-hour clock starts at the acceptance timestamp, not at sync. [load-bearing] Medium Confirm legal/ops interpretation in writing
A10 Audit history is required to be retained after local customer data is purged, i.e. purge must delete PII while leaving pseudonymous audit entries intact or retained server-side. [load-bearing] Medium Written confirmation from compliance
A11 Photos and signatures are immutable once captured; inspectors correct a bad photo by adding another, not by editing. High Confirm with one inspector during field visit
A12 The app already has authenticated session/token handling sufficient for background sync, and token lifetime can be extended or renewed without user interaction for at least the offline window. Medium Inspect auth module; see D5
A13 Device clock may be wrong or skewed; clients cannot be trusted for ordering. High N/A — design treats it as true
A14 The web/supervisor editor is online-only, so all supervisor edits pass through the server and get a version bump. High Confirm with web team
A15 Lost/stolen devices can be remotely wiped by MDM, which is the backstop for the 24-hour purge requirement. Medium Confirm MDM supports selective/full wipe

3. User flow

3.1 Pre-work (online or on any connectivity)

  1. App syncs: pulls assigned inspections, their pinned form templates, and site metadata.
  2. Inspector taps "Go offline" (or the app auto-prepares). App reports readiness: N inspections ready, storage available for M photos, last sync T ago.
  3. App refuses to go offline if a required inspection has an unresolved blocking conflict, or if projected storage is insufficient.

3.2 Offline

  1. Inspector opens an inspection from the local list. Banner: Offline — changes saved on this device.
  2. Form, photos, and signature are written transactionally to SQLite and to a durable outbox in the same transaction. UI never writes to the network path.
  3. Per-inspection footer shows pending state: 12 changes, 4 photos, 1 signature not yet uploaded.
  4. Inspector taps Complete → record moves to pending_sync locally. It is not accepted server-side; acceptance is a supervisor action (A9).

3.3 Reconnect

  1. Connectivity monitor fires. Sync runs pull-first, then push (§6.3): pull → detect conflicts → push outbox → upload attachments → confirm.
  2. Any blocking conflict (supervisor cancelled/reassigned/closed the inspection, or the template changed incompatibly) surfaces as a blocking task. The inspector must resolve it before that inspection can be submitted. Non-blocking field conflicts are queued for the same review and surfaced in-app; the rest of the inspection still syncs.
  3. On success the inspector sees Synced at HH:MM. The record remains on-device until the purge job removes it (§8.3).

3.4 Failure modes surfaced to the user

  • Sync partially failing (form synced, photos stuck): explicit per-item status, with a Retry action. Never a single opaque "sync failed".
  • Storage full mid-inspection: hard stop on new photo capture with a clear message and pointer to already-captured photos to delete.
  • Session expired: re-authentication is required; queued work is untouched.

4. Local data model

The cache becomes an authoritative local store. Existing cache tables are migrated (§10). All identifiers are server ids except locally-generated ones, which are UUIDv4 and are the client's permanent handle until the server assigns one.

inspections(
  id                INTEGER PK,        -- server id
  template_id       INTEGER NOT NULL,
  template_version  INTEGER NOT NULL,  -- pinned at sync time (D2)
  status            TEXT NOT NULL,     -- assigned|in_progress|pending_sync|submitted|accepted
  version           INTEGER NOT NULL,  -- last server version we know (base version)
  base_version      INTEGER NOT NULL,  -- version our local edits were made against
  site_ref          TEXT NOT NULL,     -- pseudonymous, survives purge
  site_json         TEXT,              -- PII (address, customer name) -- purged (§8.3)
  local_state       TEXT NOT NULL,     -- clean|dirty|conflicted|blocked
  assigned_to       INTEGER,
  accepted_at       INTEGER,           -- server ms, starts purge clock
  purge_after       INTEGER,           -- computed; see §8.3
  updated_at        INTEGER NOT NULL,
  deleted_at        INTEGER
)

form_records(                          -- one row per answered field
  inspection_id  INTEGER NOT NULL,
  field_id       TEXT NOT NULL,
  value_json     TEXT,
  updated_at     INTEGER NOT NULL,     -- corrected client time (§6.5)
  actor_id       INTEGER NOT NULL,
  dirty          INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  conflict_json  TEXT,                 -- supervisor's divergent value, pending review
  PRIMARY KEY (inspection_id, field_id)
)

attachments(
  local_id       TEXT PK,              -- UUIDv4 generated on capture
  inspection_id  INTEGER NOT NULL,
  server_id      INTEGER,
  kind           TEXT NOT NULL,        -- photo|signature
  sha256         TEXT NOT NULL,        -- content address; used for dedupe+idempotency
  local_path     TEXT NOT NULL,        -- app-private storage
  byte_size      INTEGER NOT NULL,
  exif_stripped  INTEGER NOT NULL,     -- §8.6
  order_index    INTEGER,
  caption        TEXT,
  state          TEXT NOT NULL,        -- pending|captured|uploading|uploaded|failed|orphan
  attempts       INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  created_at     INTEGER NOT NULL
)

signatures(
  inspection_id INTEGER PK,
  attachment_id TEXT NOT NULL,         -- immutable once captured
  signer_ref    TEXT NOT NULL,         -- pseudonymous: last-4/hash, not the raw name
  signer_name   TEXT,                  -- PII, purged with the record
  captured_at   INTEGER NOT NULL
)

outbox(                                 -- durable, ordered-per-inspection mutation queue
  seq            INTEGER PK AUTOINCREMENT,
  op_id          TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,  -- UUIDv4, idempotency key
  inspection_id  INTEGER NOT NULL,
  op_type        TEXT NOT NULL,         -- upsert_field|set_status|capture_signature|delete_photo
  payload_json   TEXT NOT NULL,
  base_version   INTEGER NOT NULL,
  attachment_ref TEXT,                  -- links upload to its metadata op
  state          TEXT NOT NULL,         -- pending|inflight|applied|rejected|conflict|abandoned
  attempts       INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  next_attempt_at INTEGER,
  last_error     TEXT
)

audit_log(                              -- append-only, mirrors server; no PII
  seq           INTEGER PK AUTOINCREMENT,
  inspection_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  op_id         TEXT NOT NULL,
  actor_id      INTEGER NOT NULL,
  actor_role    TEXT NOT NULL,          -- inspector|supervisor|system
  action        TEXT NOT NULL,
  field_id      TEXT,
  prev_hash     TEXT,                   -- hash of previous value, not the value
  new_hash      TEXT,
  client_ts     INTEGER,
  synced        INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
)

sync_state(
  key   TEXT PK,                        -- last_pull_cursor|last_success_at|server_time_offset
  value TEXT
)

conflicts(                              -- surfaced to the inspector for resolution
  id            INTEGER PK AUTOINCREMENT,
  inspection_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  field_id      TEXT,
  kind          TEXT NOT NULL,          -- blocking|field
  local_json    TEXT,
  server_json   TEXT,
  detected_at   INTEGER NOT NULL,
  resolved_at   INTEGER
)

Two invariants make this tractable:

  1. Every local mutation is captured as an outbox op in the same SQLite transaction as the state change. If the state change committed, the op exists. There is no "scan the tables and diff" reconciliation pass, which is where cache-based designs lose data.
  2. Attachments are content-addressed and immutable. A photo is never edited, so it can never conflict — it can only be missing. This removes the hardest class of conflict from the design entirely.

5. Sync protocol

5.1 Additions required to the REST API (see D1 — recommendation: build these)

The brief says the API is REST with integer record versions. Integer versions tell us that something changed but not what changed, and there is no efficient way to enumerate "everything assigned to me that changed". Two additive endpoints are needed; all existing endpoints keep working.

GET  /sync/inspections?cursor=<opaque>&limit=200
     → { items: [{ id, version, updated_at, deleted_at, template_version, status }],
         cursor, has_more, server_time }
     Cursor is an opaque (updated_at, id) tuple; stable under concurrent writes.

POST /sync/inspections/{id}/ops
     → per-op results          (batch, ordered, idempotent)
     Request:  { base_version, ops: [{ op_id, op_type, payload, client_ts }] }
     Response: { version, results: [{ op_id, status, server_value?, error?, code? }] }
               status ∈ applied | conflict | rejected | duplicate

GET  /inspections/{id}/changes?since_version=N
     → ordered field-level change entries (for field-level merge)

POST /attachments            → { attachment_id, upload_url }   (idempotent on sha256)
PUT  /attachments/{id}/chunk  → resumable chunk upload (see §7)

POST /sync/inspections/{id}/ops is deliberately per-inspection, not global: ordering guarantees are only required within an inspection, so this keeps the queue simple and lets unrelated inspections sync independently.

5.2 Pull

Opaque cursor persisted in sync_state. Paginated, resumable (cursor advances only after a page is fully applied in a transaction). Server returns server_time on every response, which the client uses to compute and persist a clock-offset correction (A13). Deletions come back as tombstones and are applied as local hard deletes after the corresponding pending ops are resolved (§6.2, deletion row).

5.3 Order of operations per sync cycle

1. pull (cursor)            → apply, record conflicts, update base_version
2. resolve blocking conflicts → if any, stop; require user action
3. push outbox ops (batch, per inspection, ordered by seq)
4. upload attachments (metadata op first, then bytes; see §7)
5. confirm: clear applied ops, update sync_state, emit metrics
6. schedule purge job (§8.3)

Pull before push is intentional: it surfaces conflicts before we spend a slow, metered upload on data that we already know will be rejected or merged.

5.4 Push semantics and idempotency

  • Every op carries a client-generated op_id (UUIDv4) and the base_version it was authored against.
  • The server keeps (op_id → result) for a bounded retention window (recommend 30 days, D4) and returns the original result for a replayed op_id rather than re-applying it. This is what makes retries safe on flaky connections, where a request may have succeeded but the response was lost.
  • Batch results are per-op, not all-or-nothing: one poisoned op does not block the other 40. Ops that come back rejected with a permanent code (validation, permission) are moved to abandoned, surfaced to the user, and never retried.
  • Ops that come back applied are deleted from the outbox only after the server's new version is committed locally; otherwise a crash between response and commit replays the op harmlessly via the idempotency table.

5.5 Retry, backoff, and partial connectivity

  • Exponential backoff with full jitter: min(cap, base * 2^attempt) randomised, capped; honour Retry-After when present; reset the attempt counter on a successful cycle.
  • A request with no response is retried as-is (safe by idempotency). A request that returned 5xx mid-body is safe to retry because application only happens on response commit.
  • Intermittent connectivity is expected: the sync loop is chunked and interruptible. It makes progress per inspection and per attachment, persists that progress, and resumes. A cycle that dies at 30% leaves 30% durably synced.
  • Battery/storage-aware: defer photo upload while on battery below a threshold unless the user forces it; surface that as a user-visible choice (D6).

5.6 Concurrency guards

  • Exactly one sync coordinator process at a time, enforced by a SQLite lease row with an expiry — prevents the UI, the background worker, and a foreground retry from double-uploading.
  • All sync writes occur in explicit transactions with WAL mode; no long-held transactions across network calls.

6. Conflict policy

Supervisors edit the same inspection from the web. The brief rules out a collaborative editor, so we need a deterministic, explainable policy — not a merge UI for everything.

6.1 Principle

Never silently drop either side's work. Where automatic resolution is defensible we apply it and record it; where it is not, we preserve both values and require a human decision. Every automatic resolution is written to the audit log.

6.2 Field classes and precedence

Class Examples Rule
Inspector-authored answers measurements, notes, pass/fail Inspector wins while status ∈ {assigned, in_progress}. If the supervisor changed the same field since our base_version, both values are preserved in conflicts for review — we do not pick a winner.
Supervisor/structural fields assignee, scheduled date, status transitions, cancellation Server authoritative. The tablet never originates these; it only renders them.
Post-acceptance edits any field, after accepted Supervisor wins. The tablet shows the record read-only; local divergent values go to conflicts as evidence, not as an edit.
Attachments photos, signature Append-only, content-addressed, immutable → cannot conflict, only fail to upload.
Deletion inspection or photo deleted Hard delete / erasure requests always win; sync of pending edits to a deleted record is abandoned with a blocking notice.

6.3 Automatic resolution within a class

Where both sides changed a single-value field and the class says the inspector wins, we use the later of the corrected timestamps (§5.2), with the losing value preserved in conflicts for 30 days. Text/notes fields are never auto-merged by string diffing; divergence is always a human decision.

6.4 Blocking vs non-blocking

  • Blocking: supervisor cancelled/reassigned/closed the inspection; template version changed incompatibly (D2); a required field was removed. The inspection cannot sync until resolved. Other inspections sync normally.
  • Non-blocking: field-level divergences. The inspection syncs everything else; the divergence sits in a Conflicts tray with both values side by side and a one-tap "keep mine / keep theirs / keep both as note".

6.5 Ordering and time

Integer versions give ordering per record without telling us the changed fields, so field-level merge requires either GET /changes (§5.1) or a full-record comparison on conflict. Recommendation: add the changes endpoint (D1). Time-based tie-breaks use server-corrected client timestamps: the client stamps with its own clock plus the last known server offset, never raw device time (A13).

6.6 What we deliberately do not do

No three-way text merge, no operational transformation, no per-keystroke history, no live presence. If the pilot shows field conflicts are frequent, the next investment is field-level locking/check-out (see D3 in §16), not a merge algorithm.

7. Attachments (up to 40 photos + signature)

Attachments are the heaviest part of the offline problem: A5 puts worst-case raw capture at hundreds of MB per inspection, and A6 says the return path is slow.

  1. Capture. Photo written to app-private storage immediately, EXIF/GPS stripped at capture time (§8.6), sha256 computed, attachments row created in the same transaction as the outbox metadata op. Capture never waits for the network.
  2. Optimisation. A transcode/thumbnail pass runs when the device is idle and charging (or immediately if the user is in a hurry), producing a "sync-quality" derivative. Recommendation: upload the sync-quality derivative by default and retain the original locally until the record is accepted and purged, so no resolution is lost permanently by accident; make "original or optimised" a policy setting (D8).
  3. Upload ordering. Metadata op first (creates server_id), then bytes. The attachment_ref on the outbox op links them, so an orphaned upload can be retried without re-sending metadata.
  4. Resumable chunked upload. Chunks sized to the measured site throughput (A6, recommendation: start at 1 MB and tune from telemetry). The upload is resumable by sha256 + offset, so a mid-upload disconnect resumes rather than restarts. This is the single highest-value feature for the "40 photos over bad cellular" case.
  5. Idempotency. POST /attachments is idempotent on sha256 per inspection; a replayed request returns the existing attachment_id.
  6. Progress and fairness. Per-photo progress, sequential upload to avoid saturating a weak link with 40 parallel streams, with a bounded parallelism of 2–3 configurable by flag so we can tune it from production data.
  7. Failure handling. Per-attachment retry with backoff; after the retry budget is exhausted the attachment is failed and the inspection is marked pending_sync:photos. The form data is never blocked behind a photo upload — this is the difference between "notes reached the server" and "everything was lost".
  8. Signature. Treated as an attachment with kind=signature, uploaded with high priority (it gates completion) and immutable once captured.
  9. Storage. Before going offline the app computes projected storage for the planned inspections and refuses with a clear message if it does not fit. During capture, a low-storage threshold blocks new captures and offers deletion of the oldest uploaded photos.

8. Security and privacy

8.1 Authentication while offline

The tablet must remain usable without network, but must not become an unauthenticated data store. Recommendation (D5): app-level session unlock backed by the device credential, a session token valid for the offline window plus grace, and a hard re-auth requirement at least every N days. N is a compliance decision; the plan assumes the value comes from D5 rather than inventing one.

8.2 Data at rest

  • Encrypt the local database. The SQLite key is held in the platform keystore (Keychain/Android Keystore), not in preferences or code. Recommendation: SQLCipher or an equivalent page-level encryption layer (D9). Honest note: an encrypted database on a device whose credential is already unlocked raises the bar for a forensic or lost-device extraction; it does not protect against a compromised OS or an attacker with an unlocked device. We should not oversell it.
  • Photos and signatures live in app-private, encrypted-at-rest storage with the same threat model.
  • No customer PII in crash reports, analytics payloads, or logs — only pseudonymous site_ref / inspection_id.

8.3 The 24-hour purge (A9, A10)

Requirement: remove local customer data within 24 hours after an inspection is accepted.

  1. Clock source. purge_after = accepted_at + 24h, where accepted_at is the server timestamp received at sync — not device time (A13). This is the whole reason the pull response carries server_time.
  2. Purge scope. Delete inspections.site_json, signatures.signer_name, attachments.local_path files (photos + signature), and locally cached templates, while retaining audit_log entries that reference only site_ref, inspection_id and hashes. If compliance requires the audit history to retain the signer's identity, that identity must live server-side only, and the local audit log must record a hash rather than a name (A10). This specific interaction between purge and audit retention is the highest-risk unresolved item in the plan and must be closed in writing before M2.
  3. Execution. A purge job runs on every app foreground, on every successful sync cycle, and via a periodic background worker. It is idempotent, records a completion event, and emits purge_overdue_age_hours if any record is past due.
  4. Verification, not just implementation. A test asserts that after purge no PII remains in the database file, the file system, and any WAL/-shm/journal sidecar files. Deleting rows without VACUUM/secure-delete can leave recoverable data in free pages — this is a known failure mode and must be covered explicitly.
  5. Backstop. MDM remote wipe (A15) for lost/stolen devices, plus wiping the keystore key on too-many-failed-unlock attempts.

8.4 Transport and server

TLS everywhere, certificate pinning only if the ops team owns the pin-rotation runbook (it is a self-inflicted outage waiting to happen otherwise). Server-side authorisation re-validated at sync time, not just at capture time: an inspector who was unassigned while offline cannot push ops to that inspection (§6.2, supervisor fields are authoritative).

8.5 Tamper-evidence

Audit log rows are append-only locally; the local log mirrors the server and is not the system of record. Each op carries op_id and actor, and value hashes chain (prev_hash → new_hash) so the server can detect an out-of-order or missing op.

8.6 Other

  • EXIF/GPS stripped at capture (privacy + it also shrinks files).
  • Background work rate-limited and battery-aware, because a sync loop that drains the battery is a sync loop inspectors will disable.

9. Migration and backfill

9.1 Client

  • Versioned, forward-only SQLite migrations (user_version), each with a down-guard: the app refuses to open a database newer than itself and falls back to wipe-and-rehydrate, which is acceptable today because the store is only a cache — and will stop being acceptable once it is authoritative. From M1 onward, migrations must be non-destructive and must never drop the outbox.
  • Migration order: create new tables → backfill from cache tables → dual-write period → switch reads → drop legacy cache tables behind a flag.
  • Critical constraint: any release that can go out with pending outbox ops must drain the outbox before applying a destructive migration, or pending notes are destroyed. This is enforced by a blocking pre-migration check, not by convention.
  • Roll-forward is the default posture for schema changes; the flag (§12) controls behaviour, not schema.

9.2 Server

  • Backfill version, updated_at, deleted_at for existing records; confirm the version column is bumped for every existing write path including supervisor edits (A8) — a missed increment is invisible until it silently overwrites data.
  • Backfill retroactive audit entries for in-flight inspections, marking them source=backfill so the audit history is honest about provenance.
  • Add idempotency and change-log tables; backfill is not required for the sync endpoints because clients start from a known cursor at first sync.
  • Pin template versions and start recording them on inspections (D2), so an offline tablet always renders the schema it captured against.

10. Observability

Metrics (all sliced by app version, rollout stage, and inspection):

  • sync_cycle_success_rate, sync_cycle_duration_p50/p95/p99
  • outbox_depth (gauge) and outbox_oldest_op_age_hours — the data-loss early warning; alert on backlog age crossing a threshold, not just on error rate
  • op_result_total{status} (applied/conflict/rejected/duplicate)
  • conflict_rate overall and per field id — the latter tells you which form field is badly designed
  • attachment_upload_success_rate, upload_duration_p95, upload_retry_total, orphaned_attachments
  • purge_success_total, purge_failure_total, purge_overdue_age_hours (alert: any record past 24h), pii_rows_after_purge (must be 0)
  • time_since_last_successful_sync (validates A2), offline session duration
  • local_db_size_bytes, free_storage_bytes, sync_battery_drain_pct
  • Crash-free sessions, sync-worker ANR/watchdog terminations

Logging: structured events with device_id, inspection_id, op_id, attempt, base_version, server_version, and error code. No PII, ever (§8.2). Ops are logged by op_id so a support ticket from a basement can be traced end to end.

Tracing: a sync-cycle trace per attempt spanning pull → conflict → push → upload, with attachment upload as child spans, so "why did this take 9 minutes" is answerable.

Dashboards: pilot health (per-inspector backlog age, sync success, purge compliance), conflict analysis (which fields, which supervisors), attachment performance.

Alerting: backlog age, purge overdue/failed, conflict rate spike, upload success rate drop, sync cycle stuck. Each alert names its owner and its first diagnostic step.

11. Testing strategy

  1. Unit. Outbox reducer, op application/rollback, idempotency replay, conflict resolver per field class (table in §6.2 as executable cases), purge scope and completeness, clock-offset correction, storage projection.
  2. Integration against a fake server harness. Deterministic fault injection is the core of this plan's confidence: latency, 5xx, truncated responses, response-lost- after-commit (the classic duplicate-write bug), partial batch results, out-of-order ops, duplicate op_id, tombstone racing a pending edit.
  3. Property/permutation tests. Random op orderings and interleavings with concurrent supervisor edits; invariant: no acknowledged write is lost, and the client and server converge to the same final state for any permutation.
  4. On-device / system tests (the ones that actually find offline bugs). Airplane mode for a full inspection; connectivity flapping every few seconds; kill the app mid-upload and mid-sync; background the app during sync; run out of storage mid-capture; device clock skewed hours; low battery; app upgrade with a non-empty outbox; token expiry mid-sync.
  5. Scale/perf. 40 photos per inspection, largest realistic inspection, oldest device in the fleet; measure sync wall time, battery drain, DB growth and query latency over a simulated multi-week history.
  6. Security/privacy. Static analysis of storage paths; a purge verification test that greps the database file, WAL files, and the file system for known PII canaries; review of log/analytics payloads for PII leakage.
  7. Manual field test. Real inspectors in a real basement with no signal, on the oldest supported tablet, before the pilot. Non-negotiable — no lab test reproduces the actual environment described in the brief.
  8. Regression guard. A permanent "offline golden path" suite that runs on every release candidate: go offline → complete inspection → reconnect → verify server state.

12. Staged rollout

Feature-flagged end to end. Every stage has an explicit exit gate; no stage advances on elapsed time alone.

  • Stage 0 — Shadow mode (internal). The sync engine writes to the outbox and reads locally, but all reads still come from the network and writes go through the existing endpoints. Purpose: validate the outbox and the new endpoints under real load with zero user-visible behavior change. Exit: outbox write path has no crashes, new endpoints are within latency budget, and shadow writes reconcile cleanly against the primary path.
  • Stage 1 — Internal dogfood. Engineering/QA use offline mode on real inspections that are later discarded or carefully reviewed. Kill switch verified. Exit: all stage-1 acceptance criteria in M3 met; purge verified manually on a real device.
  • Stage 2 — Limited pilot. A small, volunteer group of inspectors in one region with a supervising contact on standby. Daily triage of sync failures and a named rollback owner. Exit: pilot exit criteria (below) met for a sustained period, and zero data-loss or purge-breach incidents.
  • Stage 3 — Expanded pilot. More inspectors and a second region, specifically to exercise the supervisor-edit conflict path at realistic volume. Exit: conflict rate and resolution time within target; no blocking conflicts unresolved.
  • Stage 4 — Broad rollout. Flag on by default, staged by region with a canary percentage. The kill switch stays in place.

Pilot exit criteria (definition of "the pilot worked"):

  1. Zero confirmed incidents of acknowledged inspector input lost.
  2. 100% of accepted inspections purged within 24 hours (measured, from telemetry — not asserted).
  3. Sync success rate and p95 sync duration at or better than the agreed target.
  4. Field-conflict rate low enough that the conflict tray is not a daily burden; blocking conflicts explained and handled.
  5. Inspectors complete inspections offline at least as fast as online.

13. Rollback

The rollback risk is asymmetric: turning the feature off eagerly can destroy pending work. Therefore rollback is two-phased.

  1. Phase A — Drain mode (always run first). Flag flips to drain: the app stops accepting new offline edits, pushes everything in the outbox, confirms, and only then reverts to online-only. No pending data is ever discarded by a rollback.
  2. Phase B — Hard disable. Online-only read-through-cache behavior, identical to today's app. Used only after the outbox is empty, or in an emergency where retaining data is judged less important than stopping harm.

Rollback triggers (examples; final list agreed before Stage 1):

  • Any confirmed loss of acknowledged input.
  • Any purge breach past 24 hours.
  • Sync success rate below threshold for a sustained period.
  • Crash-free-session regression attributable to the offline stack.
  • Data-integrity errors (version mismatches, audit-log gaps) above rate zero.

Notes:

  • Server-side additions are additive and independently deployable, so server rollback does not require client rollback; old clients simply never call the new endpoints.
  • Client rollback is complicated by §9.1: once the store is authoritative, force-killing the app to an older build must not wipe a non-empty outbox. Blocks are enforced in the migration path.
  • Rollback does not un-retire data. If a purge already ran, it cannot be undone; this is why the purge job is gated behind stage-2 verification rather than enabled at stage 0.

14. Milestones

Sequenced with dependencies. No calendar dates and no staffing estimates — these are commitments the team should size; the plan's job is to make the order and the blocking relationships explicit. Each milestone lists the acceptance criteria that gate moving on.

M0 — Assumptions closed and decisions made

Depends on: nothing. Work: validate A1–A15 (§2); get written answers to D1–D10 (§16); measure photo sizes, storage headroom, and site throughput; confirm compliance interpretation of A9/A10. Acceptance: all [load-bearing] assumptions have measured evidence or a named owner; every decision in §16 has a recorded answer; scope boundaries in §1 signed off. Blocks: M1 (cannot pick the sync contract while D1 is open).

M1 — Local authoritative store and outbox (no sync yet)

Depends on: M0. Work: schema migrations (§4, §9.1); transactional write path where every mutation produces an outbox op; offline-capable UI states; storage projection and low-storage handling; encryption at rest (D9). Acceptance: airplane-mode golden path — open inspection, fill 50 fields, capture 40 photos, capture signature, kill the app, reopen, all data present; automated test proves no code path mutates state without an accompanying outbox op; PII encrypted at rest verified. Blocks: M2, M3.

M2 — Server sync endpoints

Depends on: M1 (and M0's D1 answer). Work: GET /sync/inspections with opaque cursor; POST /sync/inspections/{id}/ops with per-op results and idempotency; GET /changes; attachment endpoints; server backfill (§9.2); auth/authorisation re-validation at sync time (§8.4). Acceptance: idempotency replay returns the original result; concurrent supervisor edit + client push yields a deterministic, audited outcome; load test at projected fleet volume; backfill reconciles 100% of existing records. Blocks: M3.

M3 — Client sync engine, conflict resolution, and attachment upload

Depends on: M2. Work: sync coordinator with lease (§5.6); pull/push order (§5.3); retry/backoff (§5.5); chunked resumable upload (§7); conflict detection, the conflicts table and the resolution tray (§6); telemetry (§10). Acceptance: every fault in the integration harness is survived with no data loss; kill-the-app-mid-upload resumes; 40-photo inspection uploads over a throttled link and completes; the permutation suite converges for all tested interleavings; dashboards live. Blocks: M4.

M4 — Purge, security hardening, and compliance evidence

Depends on: M3. Work: purge job + verification + overdue alerting (§8.3); PII-in-logs audit; secure deletion of DB free pages; MDM/remote-wipe integration; security review and penetration test; session/re-auth policy (D5). Acceptance: canary-PII test proves zero PII remains in DB, WAL, and file system after purge; purge_overdue_age_hours alerting verified end to end; security findings triaged with no open high-severity items. Blocks: M5.

M5 — Pilot (Stage 2), measurement, and exit decision

Depends on: M4, plus the manual field test and the M1/M3 regression guards. Work: Stage 0/1 exits; limited pilot with daily triage; conflict-rate tracking; collect pilot exit criteria evidence (§12). Acceptance: all five pilot exit criteria met; go/no-go recorded with the data behind it; rollback rehearsed once, not just documented. Blocks: broad rollout (Stage 3/4).

15. Risk register (top items)

Risk Why it matters Mitigation
Purge deletes audit data (or audit retention defeats purge) Direct regulatory breach either way Resolve A10 in writing at M0; retain hashes + pseudonymous refs locally; purge verification test
Outbox destroyed by an app upgrade Silent data loss — exactly the bug the feature exists to fix Destructive migrations blocked while outbox is non-empty (§9.1); upgrade-with-pending-ops system test
Photo volume overwhelms slow links Inspection never finishes syncing; inspectors lose trust Optimised derivatives, resumable chunks, bounded parallelism, per-item status, tune from telemetry
Version increments missed on some server write path Client overwrites supervisor edits silently Audit counters on every write path; canary job comparing version to updated_at
Conflict rate higher than assumed Tray becomes daily overhead; product asks for a merge editor Per-field conflict metrics from day one; fallback is field check-out/locking, not a merge algorithm (D3)
Clock skew corrupts purge/tie-breaks Wrong purge timing, wrong conflict winner Server-time offset persisted on every pull; never trust raw device time

16. Decisions required before implementation (with recommendations)

These must be answered in M0; each one changes code, not just wording.

D1 — Can we add sync-specific endpoints to the server API? Recommendation: yes, add three additive endpoints (§5.1). Integer per-record versions alone cannot support field-level merge or an efficient delta pull; without new endpoints we are forced into last-write-wins on whole records, which will discard supervisor or inspector work. Keeping them additive means zero migration risk for existing clients. If refused: fall back to whole-record LWW with If-Match: version, and accept that concurrent edits lose data — this should be a written, signed-off product decision.

D2 — How do we handle form template changes while a tablet is offline? Recommendation: pin template_version on the inspection at sync time; the tablet renders the pinned schema. On reconnect, if the template changed, treat it as a non-blocking review item for additive/compatible changes and a blocking item when a field the inspector answered was removed or retyped. Never silently re-map answers to a schema they were not captured against.

D3 — What happens when supervisor and inspector edit the same field? Recommendation: preserve both, auto-resolve only where precedence is unambiguous (§6.2). Specifically: inspector wins pre-acceptance, supervisor wins post-acceptance, and ambiguous divergences go to a human. If the conflict rate turns out to be high, the next investment should be whole-inspection check-out (a soft lock while an inspector is offline), not a merge algorithm — this matches "no full collaborative editor".

D4 — How long should the server retain idempotency keys? Recommendation: 30 days, with the practical requirement that it exceeds the maximum credible offline window plus retry tail (A2). Enforce it as a monitored invariant: alert if any incoming op_id is older than the retention window.

D5 — How long may a tablet stay offline before re-authentication is required? Recommendation: device-credential-backed app unlock plus a server-defined maximum offline period, after which syncing requires online re-auth; the exact value comes from compliance, not from this plan. Do not ship with an unbounded offline window on a device holding customer PII.

D6 — When should photo upload run? Recommendation: automatic on any connectivity, deferred while on low battery, with an explicit user override ("upload now"). Also offer "upload on Wi-Fi only" for inspectors on metered cellular — with the honest caveat that it delays the purge clock only if acceptance happens before upload, which is why upload should be gated on connectivity, not on network type, by default.

D7 — Cross-device continuation: in or out? Recommendation: out for the pilot. Supporting it means distributing the authoritative local state across devices, which is a materially harder problem. Handle the practical case operationally for the pilot: an inspection started on the wrong tablet gets reassigned by a supervisor.

D8 — Do we upload originals or optimised derivatives? Recommendation: optimised derivative by default, original retained locally until purge, configurable per policy. Evidence first: measure actual file sizes (A5) and the evidentiary requirement for photos before locking this in — if originals are legally required, the storage plan (§7, item 9) and the upload budget change substantially.

D9 — What encryption do we use for the local database? Recommendation: SQLCipher (or equivalent page-level encryption) with the key in the platform keystore. Accept the stated limit (§8.2) and do not market it as stronger than it is. Verify it against the fleet's oldest hardware for performance impact before committing.

D10 — Who owns the "accepted" timestamp, and what exactly counts as customer data? Recommendation: the server owns accepted_at, and the purge scope is fixed as an explicit, enumerated field list in code (§4 tables) rather than a vague table-wide delete. Get the enumerated list reviewed by compliance at M0 and turn it into a test fixture. This is the cheapest place to prevent a regulatory breach.

17. Summary of what is deliberately not being built

Automatic text merging; real-time co-editing; peer-to-peer sync; offline reassignment; cross-device continuation; full-record rewrite of the REST API. Each is a plausible follow-on once the pilot produces conflict-rate and volume data — none is needed to solve the problem in BRIEF.md.
