kimi-k3/06-product-planning/RESPONSE.md

RESPONSE — Three riskiest assumptions

The three riskiest assumptions in PLAN.md are:

  1. The REST/integer-version API can be extended additively without breaking existing clients (A4, decision D4). The entire sync protocol depends on server capabilities the brief does not confirm: version preconditions on writes, a 409 payload rich enough for field-level conflict resolution, idempotent photo uploads, and an incremental-pull cursor. If the server team cannot or will not add these, conflict handling degrades to record-level last-writer-wins (risking exactly the data loss the brief wants to eliminate) and push/pull becomes far chattier. This is why the API contract is gated in milestone M0 before any client or server build.

  2. Device storage and SQLite reliability are sufficient for worst-case offline loads (A3). The plan assumes roughly 200 MB per inspection (40 photos at up to ~5 MB) multiplied by the pre-download window, on company-managed tablets whose actual free space, OS background-execution limits, and database behavior under low storage are unverified. If wrong, the failure mode is severe: failed captures or corrupted outbox state in exactly the offline environments (basements) the feature targets. The plan mitigates this with compression defaults, a configurable storage floor (D8/D9), and explicit pilot verification in M1/M5, but it remains a physical constraint that no software design can fully remove.

  3. "Accepted" is a single, observable server-side transition that starts a purge clock the client can reliably honor (A5, decision D1). The 24-hour regulatory deletion requirement hinges on the client learning of acceptance in time and purging even when devices are offline for long stretches. If acceptance is ambiguous (multiple review states), or if devices routinely stay offline past the deadline, the compliance guarantee fails silently. The plan therefore treats purge-overdue detection as a server-side alert on missing receipts rather than trusting the client, and requires legal/compliance confirmation of the accepted definition and of any retroactive-purge expectations (D7) before implementation.

kimi-k3/06-product-planning/BRIEF.md

Offline inspection brief

Inspectors use company-managed tablets in basements with no signal. Today, a lost connection after opening an inspection can discard notes. They need to open assigned inspections, fill forms, take up to 40 photos, and collect a signature offline. Connectivity may return intermittently. Supervisors can edit the same inspection from the web. Regulations require an audit history and removal of local customer data within 24 hours after an inspection is accepted. Existing server APIs use REST with integer record versions. The mobile app has SQLite but currently treats it as a read-through cache. Product wants a pilot before broad rollout and does not want a full collaborative editor.

kimi-k3/06-product-planning/PLAN.md

PLAN — Offline inspection sync for tablet app

1. Context and product input

The only product input is BRIEF.md. Key facts from it:

  • Inspectors use company-managed tablets in basements with no signal.
  • Today, a lost connection after opening an inspection can discard notes.
  • Required offline capabilities: open assigned inspections, fill forms, take up to 40 photos per inspection, collect a signature.
  • Connectivity may return intermittently.
  • Supervisors can edit the same inspection from the web.
  • Regulations require: (a) an audit history, (b) removal of local customer data within 24 hours after an inspection is accepted.
  • Existing server APIs are REST with integer record versions.
  • The mobile app has SQLite, currently used only as a read-through cache.
  • Product wants a pilot before broad rollout.
  • Product does not want a full collaborative editor.

2. Assumptions (explicit)

These are working assumptions; each is either validated in the pilot or listed as a pre-implementation decision in §14.

  1. A1 — Single-inspector ownership. An inspection is assigned to exactly one inspector at a time. Concurrent edits by two inspectors are out of scope; the realistic concurrency case is inspector (tablet) vs. supervisor (web).
  2. A2 — Assignment metadata is available online. The inspector can sync the list of assigned inspections (and the inspections themselves) while online, before going offline.
  3. A3 — SQLite on the tablet is reliable and has enough storage for a reasonable workload: brief implies ≤ 40 photos/inspection; we assume photo size ≤ ~5 MB each after compression, so ~200 MB per inspection worst case, and that devices have several GB free. To be verified during the pilot.
  4. A4 — REST/integer versions can be extended, not replaced. We can add endpoints/fields (e.g., a photo upload endpoint, a sync status endpoint, a tombstone/purge-ack endpoint) without breaking existing web clients. The server remains the system of record.
  5. A5 — "Accepted" is a server-side state transition with a timestamp the client can read, which starts the 24-hour local-purge clock.
  6. A6 — The signature is a captured image/stroke artifact plus metadata (signer name, timestamp, GPS optional), stored like a photo attachment, not a cryptographic e-signature product.
  7. A7 — Audit history is primarily server-side. The client must not destroy information needed for audit; every mutation is attributable to a user and a device. The client keeps a local audit log only until it is uploaded.
  8. A8 — Devices are company-managed, so MDM features (device encryption enforcement, remote wipe, app pinning) are available.
  9. A9 — Intermittent connectivity is short-burst and low-bandwidth (e.g., briefly surfacing from a basement). Sync must be incremental and resumable, not all-or-nothing.
  10. A10 — Existing read-through cache schema is disposable. There is no production data in the local SQLite that must be preserved; migration is schema migration, not data rescue. (To be confirmed.)

3. Goals and success criteria

Goal: an inspector can complete an entire inspection — open, fill forms, up to 40 photos, signature — with zero connectivity, and lose nothing when connectivity drops or the app is killed.

Success criteria (measured in the pilot):

  • Zero reported data loss of notes/photos/signature across app restarts and network loss (target: 0 incidents).
  • 100% of completed offline inspections eventually reach the server without manual intervention once connectivity returns.
  • Local customer data purged within 24 h of acceptance on 100% of devices that check in; purge failures are detected and alerted, not silent.
  • Conflict rate (inspector edit vs. supervisor edit on same record) is measured and the conflict UX resolves 100% of them without data loss.

4. User flow

4.1 Inspector

  1. Prepare (online): inspector opens the app on Wi‑Fi/cellular. App syncs the assigned-inspection list and pre-downloads the full inspection payloads (form definitions, current record versions, existing photos) for the next N days (N configurable, default: today's and tomorrow's assignments).
  2. Work (offline-capable): inspector opens an assigned inspection, fills the form section by section, takes photos (autosaved immediately to local storage, attached to the inspection), captures the signature. Every change is written to the local database synchronously before the UI acknowledges it (write-ahead, no "save" button required; an explicit "Save" affordance may remain for UX familiarity but is a no-op confirmation).
  3. Submit: when the inspection is complete, the inspector marks it "Complete". This is a local state change queued for sync. If online, it submits immediately; if offline, it waits in the outbox.
  4. Sync (intermittent): whenever connectivity appears, a background sync worker pushes the outbox (form edits in order, then photos, then signature, then the "complete" transition), with resumable uploads. The UI shows per-inspection sync status: Local only / Syncing / Synced / Conflict / Error.
  5. Post-acceptance purge: once the server marks the inspection accepted, the next successful sync returns the accepted state; the client schedules local purge of customer data for that inspection within 24 h and reports purge completion back to the server (purge acknowledgment).

4.2 Supervisor (web)

  • Supervisors continue to use the existing web app. They see sync state of inspections (e.g., "inspector has unsubmitted offline changes" is not visible — see scope boundaries; but "submitted, awaiting review" is).
  • If a supervisor edits an inspection that the inspector has also edited offline, the conflict policy in §8 applies at the inspector's next sync.

4.3 Conflict UX

  • On a version conflict, the inspector sees the affected inspection flagged Conflict, with a field-level comparison: "your value" vs. "server value (edited by , )". The inspector picks per field (or accepts all server / keeps all mine), and the result is re-submitted. Nothing is silently overwritten either way. Supervisors are notified (web banner / email) when a conflict is resolved so they can re-review.

5. Scope boundaries

In scope:

  • Offline read of pre-synced assigned inspections.
  • Offline form editing, photo capture (≤ 40/inspection), signature capture.
  • Queue-based, resumable, background sync with conflict detection using the existing integer record versions.
  • Server-side audit history of all mutations (who/when/what/which device).
  • Local purge of customer data ≤ 24 h after acceptance, with acknowledgment and server-side tracking of purge status.
  • Pilot-first rollout with feature flag.

Out of scope (explicitly):

  • Real-time collaboration or a collaborative editor (CRDT/OT) — excluded by the brief.
  • Two inspectors editing the same inspection concurrently (A1).
  • Offline creation of new inspections on the tablet (creation stays a server/scheduler action; inspectors work only on assigned inspections).
  • Offline access to inspections not assigned to the signed-in inspector.
  • Re-assignment workflows while offline.
  • Editing photos after capture (crop/annotate) — defer unless pilot demands it.
  • Full offline web app for supervisors.
  • Background photo backup to any third-party/cloud photo service.

6. Local data model (SQLite)

Promote SQLite from read-through cache to a local system of truth for offline work, with the server as the global system of record. Draft schema (names illustrative):

  • inspection — id (server id), server_version (integer, last synced), state (assigned|in_progress|completed_local|submitted|accepted), assigned_to, payload_json (last synced server snapshot), accepted_at (server timestamp, nullable), purge_due_at, purged_at.
  • form_draft — inspection_id, field_path, value_json, base_server_version (the version the edit was made against), updated_at, updated_by_device. One row per dirty field = the outbox for form edits; preserves edit intent for conflict resolution.
  • photo — local_id (UUID), inspection_id, server_photo_id (nullable until uploaded), file_path, byte_size, sha256, capture_timestamp, upload_state (pending|uploading|uploaded|failed), upload_attempts.
  • signature — same shape as photo plus signer_name.
  • outbox_op — ordered operation log: op_id (UUID), inspection_id, op_type (upsert_fields|upload_photo|upload_signature|complete), payload_ref, created_at, state, attempts, last_error. This is the single source for "what needs to be pushed".
  • local_audit_event — append-only: event_id, timestamp, actor, device_id, inspection_id, action, detail_json, uploaded flag. Uploaded to the server audit log at sync, then eligible for local deletion at purge time.
  • sync_state — key/value: last successful pull timestamp, per-endpoint cursors, purge-ack backlog.

Notes:

  • Photos live as files in app-private storage; SQLite holds metadata and the upload queue state. SHA-256 enables dedupe and integrity checks on resume.
  • The 40-photo cap is enforced in the capture UI and matches the brief.
  • All writes that the UI confirms are committed to SQLite first (crash-safe by construction).

7. Sync protocol

Design within the constraint "REST + integer record versions".

7.1 Pull (server → client)

  • GET /inspections/assigned?since=<cursor> — returns changed assignments and current versions; client downloads full payloads for new/changed inspections (GET /inspections/{id}) including existing photo URLs.
  • Pull is incremental (cursor = server timestamp or monotonically increasing change id; recommend a server change sequence — see §14, D4).
  • Pull also returns state=accepted + accepted_at transitions, which arm the purge timer.

7.2 Push (client → server), per inspection, in outbox order

  1. PUT /inspections/{id} with header If-Version: <base_server_version> carrying the merged form fields.
    • 200 → server bumps integer version; returns new version. Client updates server_version, clears applied form_draft rows.
    • 409 Version Conflict → server returns current version + current field values (+ last editor/timestamp if available; add if missing — §14, D4). Client marks inspection Conflict, stops pushing that inspection until resolved (photos may still upload — see §8).
  2. Photo upload: POST /inspections/{id}/photos (multipart) with client UUID for idempotency (re-POST of same UUID returns the existing server_photo_id instead of duplicating). Resumable: either content-range/chunked upload or simply retry whole-file; recommend whole-file retry with server-side idempotency first, chunked upload only if pilot shows failures on large files (§14, D5).
  3. Signature upload: same as photo, typed signature.
  4. POST /inspections/{id}/complete with If-Version — transitions server state to submitted/awaiting review.
  5. Local audit events: POST /audit-events (batch, idempotent by event_id).

7.3 Sync engine behavior

  • Triggered by connectivity callbacks, app foreground, and a periodic worker (OS-permitted). Never requires user action.
  • Ordering guarantees: per-inspection FIFO; across inspections, any order.
  • Exponential backoff with jitter on 5xx/network errors; immediate surface of 4xx (auth → re-login prompt; 409 → conflict flow).
  • Partial progress is durable: every successful sub-request updates SQLite, so a dead connection mid-sync loses at most one in-flight request, which is retried idempotently.

8. Conflict policy

Given "no collaborative editor", use server-wins-by-default with explicit field-level resolution and no silent loss:

  1. Detection: integer version mismatch on push (server version > base_server_version).
  2. Automatic handling: if the supervisor's changed fields do not intersect the inspector's dirty fields, auto-merge (client rebases its edits onto the new server version and re-PUTs). This is safe because form fields are independent values.
  3. Manual handling: if fields intersect, the inspection enters Conflict state. Local edits are preserved (never discarded). Inspector resolves per field via the comparison UI (§4.3). Resolution produces a new edit set based on the latest server version and is pushed normally.
  4. Photos/signatures are additive (append-only) and never conflict.
  5. complete vs. concurrent supervisor edit: completing is allowed against the latest version after auto-merge; if the supervisor's edit materially changes the form (intersecting fields), completion is blocked until conflict resolution — so a supervisor's correction is never silently overridden by a completion.
  6. Every conflict (detected, auto-merged, manually resolved) emits audit events on both sides.

9. Attachments (photos, signature)

  • Capture: save to app-private storage immediately upon shutter/signature, before any UI confirmation; generate UUID, hash, thumbnail.
  • Limits: enforce 40 photos per inspection (brief); configurable server-side ceiling to allow future change. Signature: exactly one active per inspection; re-capture replaces the pending signature locally, but once uploaded, replacement is a new versioned artifact (audit requires history, so server keeps superseded signatures).
  • Compression: on-device resize/recompress to a configurable target (recommend default max dimension ~2000 px, JPEG ~quality 80) to bound upload size; original retained locally until purge, in case re-upload is needed (§14, D6 — confirm acceptable quality for regulatory use).
  • Integrity: SHA-256 recorded locally and sent with upload; server verifies.
  • Metadata: capture timestamp, device id; GPS optional and off by default pending privacy review (§14, D6).

10. Security

  • Data at rest: rely on managed-device full-disk encryption (A8/MDM) plus app-level encryption of the SQLite database and attachment files (e.g., SQLCipher or platform keystore-backed file encryption), because customer data lingers up to 24 h post-acceptance.
  • Data in transit: TLS only; certificate pinning optional via MDM policy.
  • Auth: existing app auth; sync endpoints require the same auth; photo URLs are signed/short-lived, not public.
  • Least data: client only ever holds assigned inspections; purge (§11) bounds retention. Failed-auth devices can be remotely wiped via MDM.
  • Audit: every mutation (create/update/complete/conflict-resolution/purge) is attributable: user id, device id, timestamp, before/after for form fields. Server audit log is append-only and outside the sync conflict domain.
  • Deletion guarantee: purge deletes local customer data: payload JSON, drafts, photos, signature, thumbnails, cached responses. Local audit rows are uploaded first, then deleted. A purge receipt is sent to the server; server tracks "devices with overdue purge" and alerts.

11. Migration and backfill

  • Client schema migration: versioned SQLite migrations from the current cache schema to the new schema. Per A10 we assume the old cache is disposable; even so, migration path: on upgrade, drop/re-create cache tables, create new tables, force a full re-pull. Verify upgrade and downgrade behavior (downgrade = old app sees unknown schema → treat as empty cache; document that downgrades lose offline drafts, and block downgrade via MDM during pilot if needed).
  • Server changes: additive only — new endpoints (photos, complete, audit-events, purge-ack), new fields (version-conflict payload, change cursor), new states. No changes to existing endpoint contracts, so web app and old app versions keep working.
  • Backfill: none required for inspections (they are created server-side already). Server-side audit log: new events start flowing at launch; no historical backfill needed. Purge tracking starts empty; only inspections accepted after launch are tracked (documented compliance boundary; if regulation requires retroactive purge verification, that is a separate workstream — flagged as D7).

12. Observability

Client (uploaded at sync, sampled for verbose logs):

  • Metrics: outbox depth, sync success/failure counts by endpoint, conflict counts (auto vs. manual), photo upload failure rate and retry counts, time from local-complete to server-submitted, purge executions and purge overdue count.
  • Structured logs with device id, app version, inspection id (hashed where privacy requires), network state transitions.

Server:

  • Metrics: version-conflict rate per inspection, 4xx/5xx on new endpoints, upload sizes/durations, audit-event ingest lag, purge-ack overdue list (device, inspection, hours overdue).
  • Alerts: purge overdue > 24 h (compliance-critical), conflict rate spike, upload failure rate spike, audit ingest failure.
  • Dashboards: pilot cohort funnel (assigned → downloaded → completed locally → submitted → accepted → purged).

13. Staged rollout and rollback

Stages (progression gated by acceptance criteria, not dates):

  1. Internal dogfood: feature-flagged build to engineering/QA devices with scripted offline scenarios.
  2. Pilot: small group of real inspectors (size chosen by product; brief requires a pilot) on managed devices, flag on, in a bounded region/team. Duration: enough to cover multiple inspection cycles; exit criteria in §15, M5.
  3. Broad rollout: ramp flag by percentage of inspectors, watching the §12 dashboards and alert thresholds at each step.

Rollback:

  • Client: the feature is behind a remote flag. Flag off = app behaves as today (online-only). Offline drafts on flagged-off devices are not deleted; they are retained and the app offers "reconnect and sync" once re-flagged, or a manual export path if the rollback is permanent.
  • Server: all changes additive, so rollback = stop routing traffic to new endpoints (flag). Existing endpoints untouched.
  • Data safety invariant: rollback must never discard an unsubmitted offline inspection. Any rollback plan that would strand drafts requires a client release that forces a final sync before disabling — gate on this.
  • Kill-switch drill: rehearse flag-off during dogfood, including the stranded-draft case.

14. Decisions required before implementation (with recommendations)

  • D1 — Definition of "accepted" and purge clock start. Which server state counts as accepted, and is the 24 h measured from accepted_at server time? Recommend: the existing "review approved" transition; clock from server accepted_at; client purges on next check-in and reports; server alerts if no purge-ack within 24 h of the device's next sync.
  • D2 — Field-level vs. record-level conflict granularity. Recommend: field-level auto-merge for non-intersecting changes, manual resolution for intersecting (§8). Record-level "server wins" is simpler but risks losing inspector work, violating the core brief.
  • D3 — Who may resolve conflicts. Inspector-only, or supervisor too? Recommend: inspector resolves (they hold the offline context); supervisor is notified and can edit again afterward.
  • D4 — Server API extensions. Confirm we may add: idempotency keys on photo POST, If-Version precondition, 409 payload with current values, change cursor for incremental pull, audit-events and purge-ack endpoints. Recommend: implement all as additive changes; they are prerequisites for M3.
  • D5 — Resumable upload strategy. Recommend: start with whole-file retry + idempotency; add chunked/resumable uploads only if pilot metrics show failures. Keeps M3 small.
  • D6 — Photo quality and metadata policy. Regulatory minimum image quality? GPS in EXIF allowed? Recommend: compressed capture at the §9 defaults pending compliance sign-off; GPS off by default.
  • D7 — Retroactive purge verification. Does the 24 h rule require evidence for inspections accepted before this feature? Recommend: treat as out of scope/compliance question to raise with legal now, not during rollout.
  • D8 — Pre-download window N. How many days of assignments to prefetch? Recommend: today + tomorrow, adjustable remotely based on pilot storage data.
  • D9 — Storage floor. Minimum free-space policy before download/capture. Recommend: block new inspection downloads below a configurable threshold and warn the inspector; verify actual device capacity in pilot (A3).

15. Milestones, dependencies, and acceptance criteria

Sequenced by dependency, not dates. No staffing estimates; effort is expressed only as order and blocking relationships.

  • M0 — Decisions and API contract. Close D1–D9; publish versioned API contract for new endpoints; compliance sign-off on D6/D7.
    • Depends on: nothing. Blocks: M1, M2, M3.
    • Acceptance: signed-off contract doc; compliance answers recorded.
  • M1 — Local offline core (client). New SQLite schema + migrations; offline open/edit/photos/signature; durable outbox; local states; no sync yet (fake transport in tests).
    • Depends on: M0. Blocks: M3.
    • Acceptance: with airplane mode on, a scripted full inspection (40 photos + signature) survives app kill and device reboot with zero loss; upgrade from current app version preserves nothing needed and never crashes (A10 verified).
  • M2 — Server sync endpoints. Additive endpoints per D4: versioned PUT, idempotent photo/signature upload, complete, audit-events, accepted-state surface, purge-ack.
    • Depends on: M0. Blocks: M3.
    • Acceptance: contract tests pass; concurrent web edit produces a 409 with usable payload; duplicate photo POST returns one record.
  • M3 — Sync engine + conflict UI (client). Pull/push engine (§7), auto-merge, conflict state + resolution UI, sync status surfaces.
    • Depends on: M1, M2. Blocks: M4.
    • Acceptance: end-to-end: offline completion syncs after reconnection; supervisor mid-edit produces auto-merge when disjoint and a resolvable conflict when intersecting; no data loss in either path; intermittent connectivity (chaos toggle every N seconds) still converges.
  • M4 — Audit, purge, observability. Server audit history for all mutations; client purge scheduler + receipts; metrics/alerts/dashboards (§12).
    • Depends on: M3. Blocks: M5.
    • Acceptance: audit trail reconstructs who/what/when/device for a full inspection lifecycle; a device with a mock-accepted inspection purges local customer data within 24 h and the server shows the receipt; an artificially blocked purge raises the overdue alert.
  • M5 — Pilot. Flag on for pilot cohort; run real inspections; collect §3 metrics.
    • Depends on: M4.
    • Acceptance (exit): zero data-loss incidents; 100% eventual sync; zero unalerted purge misses; conflict UX resolves all conflicts; inspector feedback collected; go/no-go review.
  • M6 — Broad rollout. Percentage ramp with dashboard gates; rollback drill completed beforehand.
    • Depends on: M5 exit + rollback drill (§13).
    • Acceptance: each ramp step holds §3 metrics steady for an agreed observation window before proceeding.

16. Testing strategy

  • Unit: schema migrations, outbox ordering, merge logic (disjoint vs. intersecting edits), purge scheduler time math, idempotency key handling.
  • Contract: client↔server for every new endpoint, including 409 payloads and duplicate-upload behavior.
  • Integration (device farm / emulators + real tablets):
    • airplane-mode full lifecycle; app kill mid-capture, mid-sync, mid-purge;
    • intermittent connectivity harness (toggling network on a timer) verifying convergence and no duplicate photos;
    • 40-photo stress at low storage and low battery; OS background-execution limits (verify sync completes or resumes);
    • concurrent web edit during every sync phase.
  • Compliance tests: purge timer correctness across timezone/clock skew (purge keyed to server accepted_at, not device clock); post-purge forensic check that no customer data remains in app storage; audit-log completeness.
  • Migration tests: upgrade paths from the current store; downgrade behavior documented/tested.
  • Pilot rehearsal: full dogfood of M1–M4 flows plus the rollback drill.

kimi-k3/06-product-planning/TASK.md

Task 06 — Product and engineering planning: offline inspection sync

Create PLAN.md for adding offline work to a tablet-based building inspection app. Use BRIEF.md as the only product input.

The plan should make assumptions explicit and cover user flow, scope boundaries, local data model, sync protocol, conflict policy, attachments, security, migration/backfill, observability, staged rollout, rollback, and testing. Include a milestone sequence with dependencies and acceptance criteria. Identify the decisions that must be made before implementation and offer a recommendation for each. Avoid fake dates and unjustified staffing estimates.

Write RESPONSE.md summarizing the three riskiest assumptions. Work only in this directory.

Evaluation 7.5 / 10 graded blind as submission U

A compact, coherent plan in the same vein as C/D. Acceptance is gated on a purge receipt or an enforceable lease, a strict record-level version check sends conflict packages to a supervisor, and decisions are compared with alternatives. It is careful about not relying on best-effort background jobs. But every concurrent edit, even on disjoint fields, pauses the inspector and needs supervisor resolution. Acceptance can stall, and the milestones are brief.

Strengths

  • States plainly that 'an app-only background job cannot guarantee execution while a tablet is powered off'
  • Decision log compares alternatives for draft authority, concurrency, upload, cleanup and rollout
  • Rollback keeps sync, conflict and purge paths live for devices with queued work

Weaknesses

  • Whole-inspection mismatch requires supervisor review even for disjoint fields, which is high operational burden
  • Acceptance waits for purge receipt or lease expiry; the lease mechanism is unverified
  • Thin on concrete schema, offline auth window and observability thresholds
Evidence the grader checked
  • U/PLAN.md:72 'Whole-inspection version mismatch requires review, even if the changes may be to different fields'
  • U/PLAN.md:144 deletion-clock decision
  • U/PLAN.md:118-127 milestones
  • U/RESPONSE.md: offline deletion, integer versions and server durability before purge

Objective checks

Files

gpt-6-luna/06-product-planning/RESPONSE.md

Three riskiest assumptions

  1. The 24-hour deletion rule can be enforced on a managed tablet that is offline or powered off. The brief requires local customer data removal within 24 hours after acceptance, but does not describe the tablet OS, background execution guarantees, MDM wipe/lease controls, or whether web acceptance can be delayed. If deletion depends only on the app running, this assumption may fail. The plan recommends making server acceptance wait for a purge receipt or enforceable offline-data lease expiry. Validate this behavior on the actual managed devices before the pilot; if it cannot be guaranteed, product/compliance must change the acceptance flow or clarify the requirement.

  2. Integer record versions are sufficient to prevent silent loss while inspectors and supervisors edit the same inspection. The brief confirms versioned REST APIs but not conditional-write semantics, transaction boundaries, idempotency, or any audit of web writes. The plan assumes an atomic compare-and-update, rejects stale writes, and routes the preserved local candidate to a supervisor conflict review. Confirm that all web/API write paths can participate and name the conflict resolver before implementation. Otherwise drafts could be overwritten, duplicated, or stranded.

  3. The server can durably retain the full inspection, attachments, signature, and required audit history before the tablet purges its copy. The brief requires an audit history and up to 40 photos, but does not define audit contents/retention, signature evidence requirements, upload limits, or attachment storage behavior. The plan assumes resumable, hash-verified uploads and an append-only server audit acknowledged before local deletion. Compliance/product and backend owners must agree on retention, payload limits, and signature representation before the API contract is frozen.

gpt-6-luna/06-product-planning/BRIEF.md

Offline inspection brief

Inspectors use company-managed tablets in basements with no signal. Today, a lost connection after opening an inspection can discard notes. They need to open assigned inspections, fill forms, take up to 40 photos, and collect a signature offline. Connectivity may return intermittently. Supervisors can edit the same inspection from the web. Regulations require an audit history and removal of local customer data within 24 hours after an inspection is accepted. Existing server APIs use REST with integer record versions. The mobile app has SQLite but currently treats it as a read-through cache. Product wants a pilot before broad rollout and does not want a full collaborative editor.

gpt-6-luna/06-product-planning/PLAN.md

Offline inspection sync plan

Status: Proposed plan for implementation planning
Product input: BRIEF.md only. Details not stated there are marked as assumptions or decisions.
Goal: Let an inspector complete an assigned building inspection when disconnected, retain the work through intermittent connectivity, and sync it without silently overwriting a supervisor's changes.

Understanding summary

  • Inspectors use company-managed tablets in basements with unreliable or absent signal.
  • They need to open assigned inspections, complete forms, take up to 40 photos, and capture a signature offline.
  • Work must survive connection loss and app restarts; connectivity may return intermittently.
  • Supervisors may edit the same inspection through the web app.
  • Existing server APIs are REST-based and use integer record versions; the mobile app already has SQLite but currently uses it as a read-through cache.
  • An inspection's local customer data must be removed within 24 hours after it is accepted, and the server must retain an audit history.
  • The pilot should add dependable offline work without turning the product into a full collaborative editor.

Recommended design

Promote SQLite from a read-through cache to the durable local workspace for the inspector's assigned draft. Save each form change and an ordered outbox event in one local transaction before showing it as saved. Keep the server's integer version as the optimistic concurrency token. Sync queued draft changes and attachments idempotently when connectivity permits. If the server version has advanced, preserve both versions and stop automatic writes; send a conflict package for supervisor review rather than merging or overwriting data silently.

Treat server acceptance as a final server-side state transition. The tablet must first upload and receive durable acknowledgments for the inspection, audit events, signature, and attachments, then delete its customer data and per-inspection key and send a purge receipt. Only then should the server finalize acceptance. For a tablet that is offline when a supervisor attempts acceptance, acceptance must wait for a purge receipt or an enforceable offline-data lease to expire. This is the recommended way to make the 24-hour rule meaningful; confirm the platform and MDM can support it before pilot.

Assumptions and constraints

These are planning assumptions, not additional facts from the brief:

  1. Offline creation is limited to assigned inspections already downloaded to that tablet while online. New assignments and unassigned customer records are not available offline.
  2. One inspector owns a local working copy at a time. A user switch, sign-out, or reassignment must first sync or safely retain the current draft and must not expose it to another user.
  3. A server-side accepted state is the compliance clock's start. A local “ready to submit” action while offline is not yet acceptance.
  4. The server can add endpoints and tables compatibly, enforce the existing integer version in a transaction, and retain append-only audit events.
  5. The managed tablet platform can encrypt local database/files, exclude them from consumer/cloud backups, and support a reliable local purge or a managed-device recovery path. This needs verification; an app-only background job cannot guarantee execution while a tablet is powered off.
  6. “40 photos” is a maximum per inspection, with the signature stored as a separate artifact. File size, supported image formats, and compression quality remain to be decided.
  7. Audit retention duration, audit contents, signature evidentiary requirements, and conflict-resolution ownership need approval from the relevant product/compliance owners before implementation.

User flow and states

  1. Prepare: While connected, the inspector opens an assigned inspection. The app downloads its current form, assignment, integer server_version, and required reference data. It writes an encrypted local baseline and working copy before making the inspection available offline.
  2. Work offline: Form edits autosave to SQLite transactionally. Each edit is also placed in a durable, ordered outbox. The UI shows local save status separately from server sync status. Photos and the signature are saved in encrypted app storage and referenced by local metadata. The app enforces the 40-photo limit.
  3. Reconnect: Connectivity is only a hint to try sync. The app resumes queued changes and interrupted attachment uploads with exponential backoff and jitter. A successful network request is acknowledged by its idempotency key; retries do not create duplicate edits, audit events, or attachments.
  4. Version conflict: If the server version differs from the draft's base version, the app pauses automatic writes and acceptance. It preserves the local draft and attachments, fetches the current server version, and creates an isolated conflict package. A supervisor reviews the local candidate and canonical server record in a minimal web conflict workflow, then records a resolution. This is exception handling, not live co-editing.
  5. Submit and accept: After required fields, photos, and signature are present, the inspector submits. The server validates assignment and version, persists the final data and audit history, and confirms all artifact uploads. It returns a ready_to_accept receipt. The client removes the inspection's local data and key, then sends an idempotent purge receipt. The server marks the inspection accepted only after that receipt, or after an approved, enforceable device-lease expiry path. The app retains only a non-customer-data tombstone/receipt.
  6. Cleanup: If acceptance is initiated from the web while a tablet still holds an offline copy, the server does not finalize acceptance until that tablet reports purge or its enforceable lease expires. The client also runs cleanup on launch and scheduled background opportunities. Cleanup removes database rows, journal/outbox payloads, photos, thumbnails, signatures, upload staging files, SQLite WAL/journal files, and encryption keys.

Suggested states are assigned_cached → in_progress_local → queued → syncing → conflict_review (when stale) or ready_to_accept → purged_pending_receipt → accepted. The state shown to the user must distinguish “saved on this tablet,” “synced,” and “accepted.”

Scope boundaries

In scope: assigned inspections; offline form entry; up to 40 photos; offline signature capture; local durable autosave; queued/idempotent sync; optimistic version checks; a bounded supervisor conflict-review/resolution path; server audit events; secure local storage and purge; rollout and operational telemetry.

Out of scope for this pilot: offline access to every customer or inspection; creation of assignments offline; simultaneous live editing, chat, presence, comments, or general-purpose field-level merge; unlimited media; synchronization across multiple inspector devices; a broad redesign of the supervisor web experience. The minimal web conflict workflow exists only to resolve a stale-version submission safely.

Local data model

Use additive, transactional SQLite schema migrations. Store customer data only for active assigned inspections.

Entity Key fields and purpose
inspection_workspace inspection_id, assignment_id, inspector_id, base_server_version, encrypted base_snapshot, encrypted working_snapshot, state, local_updated_at, accepted_at/purge_due_at when known. The baseline enables stale-version review; the working snapshot is the durable offline draft.
outbox_event Stable event_id/idempotency key, inspection ID, monotonic per-inspection sequence, base version, event type, encrypted change payload, actor/device identity, client timestamp, retry state. Keep events ordered per inspection.
attachment Opaque attachment ID, inspection ID, kind (photo or signature), encrypted local file reference, byte count, content hash, capture time, ordering, upload session/state. Derivatives and temporary chunks are also customer data.
cleanup_tombstone Opaque inspection identifier, purge receipt ID, server acceptance time, and cleanup outcome only. It must not contain form values, customer identity, photos, signature data, or queued payloads.

The server remains authoritative for canonical accepted inspections and audit history. SQLite is authoritative for the not-yet-accepted local draft on that device. Never treat a stale cache row as a valid offline assignment without server-issued assignment/version metadata.

Sync protocol and conflict policy

  1. Bootstrap: Fetch an assigned inspection snapshot plus integer version and assignment authorization. Store baseline and working copy atomically. The server must reject changes from revoked or unauthorized assignments.
  2. Persist before acknowledging locally: On each edit, update the working snapshot and append its outbox event in one SQLite transaction. A local “saved” indicator appears only after commit. A crash or force-quit must leave either both records or neither.
  3. Send in order: Submit events per inspection with a stable idempotency key and base_version/If-Match integer version. Server validation, canonical update, version increment, and audit append happen atomically. Return the new version and event acknowledgment. Retry of an acknowledged key returns the original result.
  4. Upload artifacts: Create an upload session, send resumable chunks (or a resumable equivalent supported by the chosen REST service), validate final byte count and SHA-256 digest, then attach the server artifact ID to the inspection. Do not report final submission complete while any artifact is incomplete.
  5. Stale version: Return a typed conflict response with current version. Do not apply any part of a stale write. The app pauses later events for that inspection and preserves its local state. A separate conflict endpoint stores the local candidate against its base and observed server versions without changing the canonical inspection. The minimal supervisor workflow compares the two versions and commits a deliberate resolution as a new version with its own audit event. The inspector can then continue from that resolved version if work remains.
  6. No automatic merge in the pilot: Whole-inspection version mismatch requires review, even if the changes may be to different fields. This makes behavior predictable for regulated forms and avoids assuming field-level merge rules that the brief does not define. No signature is silently replaced or merged.
  7. Acceptance: Server verifies required form state, the signature, all artifact hashes, authorization, and audit persistence. It issues ready_to_accept; the client purges local customer data and keys and posts an idempotent purge receipt. Server transitions to accepted and records the acceptance time only under the agreed purge/lease policy.

Attachments and signature

  • Enforce no more than 40 photo artifacts per inspection; count pending, uploaded, and retried photos consistently so retries cannot bypass the limit.
  • Persist each capture to encrypted local storage before showing it as attached. Keep stable attachment IDs across retries. Show upload state per item and allow a failed transfer to resume without taking the photo again.
  • Use resumable uploads with checksum verification. The API must define allowed formats, maximum bytes per file and inspection, image-processing rules, chunk/session expiry, and server retention of abandoned uploads before implementation.
  • Treat signatures as separate protected evidence. Preserve the captured artifact and capture metadata; do not edit or merge it during conflict handling. Confirm signer attribution, consent wording, timestamp requirements, and whether the server needs the original stroke data, a rendered image, or both.
  • Delete originals, previews, transformed copies, chunks, and server-side abandoned conflict artifacts according to the approved retention policy. Never put image or signature content in logs.

Security, audit, and deletion

  • Encrypt SQLite and all inspection files at rest with per-inspection data keys protected by the managed OS keystore. Require the tablet's normal device authentication to access app data. Exclude the database, files, and keys from unmanaged backups. Use TLS and server-side authorization for every sync, upload, conflict, and acceptance request.
  • Bind queued work to the signed-in inspector, device, assignment, and stable event IDs. Revalidate authorization on receipt; do not trust client timestamps or client-provided identity by themselves.
  • The server audit is append-only and records actor/device, event ID, affected inspection/version, action, server receipt time, client event time, artifact hashes/references, and the approved before/after detail. Audit entries must be committed atomically with canonical updates and be deduplicated on retry. The exact values to retain and retention period are compliance decisions; keep audit data out of general telemetry.
  • Keep logs and metrics free of customer names, field values, photos, signatures, access tokens, and raw payloads. Use opaque IDs or pseudonyms with restricted access.
  • Prefer a purge receipt before server acceptance. If the existing business meaning requires acceptance to occur earlier, acceptance may precede deletion by at most 24 hours only if a verified platform/MDM mechanism can ensure deletion on tablets that remain offline or powered off. Do not claim compliance based solely on a best-effort app background task. Track acceptance-to-purge age and alert before the limit; escalate any breach.

Migration and backfill

  • Add server capabilities additively: idempotency, conditional version writes, audit persistence, attachment sessions, conflict packages/resolution, and acceptance/purge state. Keep existing REST callers functional during the pilot; do not reinterpret the integer version.
  • Add a forward-only, transactional SQLite migration that creates workspace, outbox, attachment, key, and tombstone structures. Test upgrade from the current read-through-cache schema and recovery from interruption.
  • On first use after upgrade, refetch active assigned inspections and their server versions; do not promote arbitrary old cache entries to offline drafts. Since the current app does not support offline work, no local offline draft history needs backfill. Remove/refetch stale cache data and immediately purge already-accepted cached customer records during upgrade.
  • No historical server inspection backfill is proposed. Existing records continue at their current versions; new audit events begin with the new audited API path. Confirm how web/API writes enter the same audit stream before enabling the pilot.
  • Deploy the additive API before the mobile feature flag. Keep old-client behavior supported until the pilot cohort is upgraded. Do not ship a downgrade path that can discard an outbox or expose a new local schema to an old app.

Observability and operations

Capture operational metadata only: sync attempts/success/failure, queue age and depth, oldest pending event, retry count, attachment bytes/progress/failure, conflict count and age, server-version rejection, duplicate idempotency hits, audit-write failures, acceptance state transitions, and acceptance-to-purge duration. Use pseudonymous device/inspection IDs and redact payloads.

Provide dashboards split by app version and pilot cohort. Alert on growing queue age, repeated upload failures, unresolved conflicts beyond the agreed service window, missing audit writes, orphaned attachment sessions, acceptance purge approaching the 24-hour limit, and any cleanup breach. Support diagnostics should expose a sync state and opaque correlation ID, not customer content. Establish retention and access controls for telemetry separately from the regulated audit store.

Staged rollout and rollback

  1. Contract and readiness: Resolve the decisions below, validate the platform/MDM purge mechanism, establish measurable pilot gates, and document a support/runbook path. No feature flag is enabled.
  2. Server dark launch: Deploy additive endpoints/schema, idempotency, audit, attachment lifecycle, and metrics without changing existing web behavior. Verify web and mobile writes are audited and version checks are atomic.
  3. Internal device cohort: Enable the new app path for managed internal tablets and test disconnected work, reconnect, conflict review, acceptance, and purge. Use synthetic or approved test records.
  4. Limited pilot: Enable an explicitly enrolled, limited cohort of inspectors/assignments. Review sync reliability, photo completion, conflict burden, audit completeness, cleanup receipts, and support feedback before expanding.
  5. Cohort expansion: Expand only after product/compliance gates are met at each step. Define numeric success thresholds from baseline and pilot data before the pilot begins; do not infer them here.
  6. Broad availability: Enable by controlled feature flag, retaining cohort and version-level monitoring and an owner/runbook for unresolved queued work.

Rollback: Turn off enrollment and new offline-workspace creation first. Keep sync, conflict resolution, and purge paths live for every device with queued work. Do not revert server audit/version data or delete queued drafts. If submission is unsafe, pause final acceptance while preserving encrypted local work and clearly surface “not accepted”; continue purge processing for already accepted inspections. Keep API changes additive and block managed app downgrade until outboxes are drained or migrated. Resume with a corrected client/server release and reconcile all pending queues before re-enabling enrollment.

Milestones, dependencies, and acceptance criteria

Milestone Depends on Acceptance criteria
M0 — Product/compliance/API decisions None Acceptance and purge semantics, audit content/retention, conflict owner/flow, artifact limits, security/MDM capability, and pilot gates are documented and approved.
M1 — Server contract and persistence M0 Version-conditional writes are atomic; idempotency retries deduplicate; audit entries are durable with each update; resumable attachments are hash-checked; stale writes return a typed conflict without changing canonical data; acceptance/purge states are queryable.
M2 — Local workspace and migration M0; API contract from M1 Upgrade from the existing cache schema is transactional; active assignments can be opened offline; every local edit survives app termination; accepted cache rows are purged; unassigned/stale cache rows cannot be opened as valid drafts.
M3 — Form sync and conflict path M1, M2 Offline edits sync in order; retries do not duplicate updates/audit entries; server version advances only on accepted writes; stale writes preserve the draft and create a supervisor-reviewable conflict without overwriting the canonical record.
M4 — Photos and signature M2, M3, attachment API in M1 The app supports 40 photos plus the separate signature artifact; interrupted upload resumes; digest mismatch or missing artifact prevents final submission; signature is preserved across retry and conflict.
M5 — Audit, purge, and telemetry M1–M4 Server audit is complete for mobile/web changes and conflict resolution; local purge removes database/WAL/outbox/media/key copies; acceptance is gated by the agreed purge policy; purge receipts and deadline breaches are observable without logging customer content.
M6 — Pilot readiness M3–M5 Migration, security, failure-mode, regression, and end-to-end scenarios pass; support runbook and rollback are rehearsed; numeric go/no-go thresholds and escalation owner are set.
M7 — Pilot and expansion M6 Pilot gate review shows no lost acknowledged edits, no silent stale overwrite, complete audit for accepted work, all accepted records within the deletion requirement, and sync/conflict/support metrics within preapproved thresholds. Expansion is explicitly approved at each cohort gate.

Test plan

  • Local persistence: Offline edits followed by process kill, device restart, low storage, and migration interruption; verify transaction boundaries, ordering, and recovery.
  • Sync/idempotency: Retry the same edit before/after a lost response; verify one canonical update and one audit event. Exercise intermittent network transitions, expired auth, server retry, and out-of-order responses.
  • Conflict: Inspector and supervisor edit concurrently; verify stale write is rejected, both candidates remain reviewable, resolution creates a new audited version, and final acceptance cannot bypass unresolved conflict.
  • Attachments: Capture 40 photos and a signature; test duplicate retries, partial/chunk interruption, hash mismatch, low storage, count boundary, cancellation, and finalization with missing media.
  • Deletion: Accept from mobile and web; exercise online, offline, powered-off, app-not-running, expired-lease, interrupted purge, duplicate receipt, and delayed server response. Verify all copies and keys are removed and the deadline is enforced by the approved platform mechanism.
  • Migration/compatibility: Upgrade from the current app cache, test old and new clients against additive APIs, confirm accepted cached rows are cleaned, and verify no existing server record is silently re-versioned or omitted from audit.
  • Security/privacy: Inspect local DB/files/backups, app logs, telemetry, and crash diagnostics for customer content; verify authorization revocation, user/device association, encrypted storage, and key destruction.
  • Operational: Dashboard/alert tests for queue backlog, conflict aging, missing audit writes, orphan uploads, and purge deadline risk. Do not use production customer content in test fixtures.

Decisions required before implementation

Decision Recommendation Why / trade-off
What starts the 24-hour deletion clock? Define acceptance as the server's final accepted transition after the client purge receipt; gate web acceptance while an offline device lease remains active. Gives the system an observable deletion point. It can delay supervisor acceptance when a tablet is unreachable, so verify lease/MDM behavior and business tolerance.
Audit detail and retention Append-only server events with actor/device, server and client times, versions, event IDs, artifact references/hashes, and approved before/after details; compliance owner sets retention before M0 closes. Supports history and deduplication; retaining field values can increase privacy and storage obligations. Do not invent a legal retention period.
Conflict handling Strict record-level version check; no automatic merge in the pilot; preserve a conflict candidate and add a minimal supervisor compare/resolve action. Prevents silent loss and avoids broad collaboration complexity; creates manual review work and requires a named resolver.
Offline availability Cache only assigned active inspections; no new assignment or broad customer search offline. Limits data exposure and keeps the offline data set bounded. Confirm assignment expiry and revocation behavior.
Photo/signature contract Cap at 40 photos, signature separate; choose maximum bytes, allowed formats, compression, and signature representation before API freeze. The brief gives a photo count but no payload/evidentiary limits. Resumable transfer is recommended for intermittent connectivity.
Device/security contract Confirm tablet OS, keystore/encryption, backup exclusion, shared-device behavior, app authentication, MDM wipe, and offline lease enforcement before pilot. A hard 24-hour physical deletion requirement cannot rest on a best-effort client task when a device may be off.
Pilot success thresholds Set numeric thresholds for sync time/reliability, conflict volume/age, storage, support burden, and purge margin from baseline before enrollment. Avoids arbitrary targets and makes expansion a reviewable decision.
API compatibility and audit coverage Add new sync APIs and ensure web writes use the same version/audit guarantees before rollout; keep existing callers compatible. Prevents a split audit history or clients bypassing version protection.

Decision log

Decision Alternatives considered Recommendation and rationale
Local draft authority Keep SQLite as cache; use memory until submit; durable local workspace Durable local workspace: it directly addresses lost notes and app/network interruption.
Concurrency Last-write-wins; automatic field merge; strict version conflict Strict version conflict for the pilot: safest with regulated forms and unknown field merge semantics.
Conflict resolution Drop local copy; overwrite server; preserve isolated candidate for supervisor review Preserve both and resolve explicitly: no silent loss or overwrite, bounded to exceptional conflicts.
Upload Single all-or-nothing payload; independent non-resumable files; resumable artifact sessions Resumable sessions with hashes: matches intermittent connectivity and up to 40 photos.
Acceptance cleanup Best-effort delete after acceptance; delay final acceptance until purge evidence Delay final acceptance until purge evidence, with a verified lease/MDM path for offline devices: gives an auditable relation between acceptance and deletion.
Rollout Big-bang update; additive dark launch and cohort flag Additive API first, then controlled cohorts: supports compatibility and a pause path without losing queued drafts.
