RESPONSE.md — Three riskiest assumptions

The plan (PLAN.md §2) lists all assumptions. These three carry the most risk: if any is wrong, core parts of the design, schedule, or compliance posture must be reworked. Each is a gating item in Milestone M0 and is validated in the pilot.

1. The existing REST + integer-version APIs can be extended to support offline sync (A1 / D1)

Assumption. Without a server redesign, the backend can add (or wrap) the semantics offline sync needs: version-preconditioned writes, a batch sync operation, client idempotency keys (mutation_id, attachment_id), client-generated UUIDs for offline-created sub-records, resumable attachment upload, and an observable accepted status with a server timestamp.

Why it's risky. The brief fixes only "REST with integer record versions." Everything downstream — the outbox/batch protocol (M4), field-level conflict merge (M5), idempotent retries over flaky links, offline attachment creation (M3), and the precise purge clock (M6) — depends on the server supporting these additions. Integer versions give optimistic concurrency, but not batching, idempotency, or an acceptance signal by themselves.

Impact if wrong. Sync degrades to sequential version-checked PATCH calls (slow in short reconnect windows, higher battery/data cost); idempotency must be bolted on client-side; conflict handling gets coarser; and the 24h purge loses its precise accepted_at origin (compounding risk #3). Schedule slips because the server contract, not just the client, changes.

Mitigation. Confirm the full API contract with the backend team in M0 before any client build; design a sequential-REST fallback (still idempotent) so the client can proceed even if batching slips.

2. Inspector and supervisor edits are largely disjoint and forms have stable field keys (A3 / D2 / D10)

Assumption. Concurrency is mostly inspector-offline vs supervisor-online on different fields/sections, and forms are normalized by stable field_key, so a field-level three-way merge resolves nearly all conflicts without a collaborative editor.

Why it's risky. The brief explicitly rules out a full collaborative editor yet requires supervisors to edit the same inspection. If, in practice, both roles edit the same fields (e.g., both adjust the same finding or note), or forms are opaque/dynamic blobs without stable keys, field-level merge breaks down.

Impact if wrong. Conflicts collapse to record-level, and the "server wins" policy would override inspector work frequently — technically not silent (audit preserves it) but operationally a data-loss/redo problem and a poor experience. At that point the "no collaborative editor" constraint is in tension with real usage, forcing either accepted overrides or scope growth.

Mitigation. Pick a pilot form with genuinely disjoint inspector/supervisor ownership (D7); measure the conflict rate and same-field-override rate in the pilot (§11) as explicit evidence for A3 before broad rollout; make per-field policy (inspector-wins / manual-review) configurable.

3. The 24-hour local purge can be guaranteed on tablets that may stay offline (A4 / D5)

Assumption. Local customer data can always be removed within 24 hours of acceptance. Deletion itself is local and needs no connectivity, but the deadline depends on the client learning the server's accepted status and accepted_at timestamp.

Why it's risky. A tablet that goes into a basement and does not reconnect again (or reconnects only after the window) may never observe accepted, so it cannot compute the exact accepted_at + 24h deadline. This is a regulatory requirement, so a miss is a compliance failure, not just a bug.

Impact if wrong. Devices could retain customer PII past the legal window, creating regulatory exposure — precisely on the managed tablets used in the field, which are also the most likely to be lost, wiped, or left offline.

Mitigation. Dual mechanism (D5): (a) status-driven purge at accepted_at + 24h when accepted is observed; (b) a conservative local TTL backstop that auto-purges customer data after a bounded time from last sync/capture so the worst case still respects 24h even if accepted is never seen; (c) MDM remote wipe as a last resort for never-returning devices. Purge runs locally (no network needed) using server-authoritative time (D8), retains a compliance receipt/tombstone, and its on-time rate is tracked as a pilot KPI with an alert on any miss. This assumption is confirmed with security/compliance in M0 and stress-tested in M6 (offline-at-deadline and never-re-synced scenarios).

qwen3.8-max/06-product-planning/BRIEF.md

Offline inspection brief

Inspectors use company-managed tablets in basements with no signal. Today, a lost connection after opening an inspection can discard notes. They need to open assigned inspections, fill forms, take up to 40 photos, and collect a signature offline. Connectivity may return intermittently. Supervisors can edit the same inspection from the web. Regulations require an audit history and removal of local customer data within 24 hours after an inspection is accepted. Existing server APIs use REST with integer record versions. The mobile app has SQLite but currently treats it as a read-through cache. Product wants a pilot before broad rollout and does not want a full collaborative editor.

qwen3.8-max/06-product-planning/PLAN.md

PLAN.md — Offline Inspection Sync

Adding durable offline work to the tablet-based building inspection app, per BRIEF.md. This plan makes its assumptions explicit, defines the design across user flow, scope, data, sync, conflicts, attachments, security, migration, observability, rollout, rollback, and testing, and lays out a dependency-ordered milestone sequence with acceptance criteria. It deliberately contains no calendar dates and no staffing numbers; sequencing is expressed through dependencies and relative complexity only.

1. Goal and success criteria

Goal. An inspector can open an assigned inspection in a no-signal basement, fill the full form, capture up to 40 photos and a signature, and have all of it survive app restarts and lost connectivity, then sync losslessly when signal returns — while supervisors can edit the same inspection from the web, an audit history is preserved, and local customer data is removed within 24 hours of acceptance.

Success criteria (measured in pilot):

  • Zero lost-notes / lost-attachment incidents across pilot sessions.
  • Offline capture survives process kill, app restart, and device reboot.
  • On reconnect, queued work drains and reconciles without user action.
  • Concurrent inspector (offline) + supervisor (web) edits reconcile with no silent data loss (overwritten values are recoverable from audit).
  • 100% of accepted inspections purge local customer data within the regulatory window, including devices that stay offline.
  • Rollback to online-only can be triggered without losing captured data.

2. Explicit assumptions

These are assumptions not stated in the brief; each is a candidate for validation in Milestone M0. The three riskiest are analyzed in RESPONSE.md.

  • A1 — Server extensibility. The REST + integer-version APIs can be extended (or wrapped) to support: version-preconditioned writes, a batch sync operation, client idempotency keys, client-generated UUIDs for offline-created sub-records, and an observable accepted status. No full server redesign is required.
  • A2 — Assignments are server-created. "Assigned inspections" already exist server-side before the inspector goes offline; the client does not need to create inspections offline, only open and edit them. Sub-records (answers, photos, signature) may be created offline.
  • A3 — Field-level mergeability. Forms have stable field keys, and inspector vs supervisor edits are largely disjoint (different field sets / sections), so most concurrency is resolvable by field-level three-way merge rather than a collaborative editor.
  • A4 — accepted is a distinct, observable state. Acceptance is a server status the client can read during sync, and it carries a server timestamp usable as the purge clock origin.
  • A5 — Managed device baseline. Tablets are company-managed with MDM (screen lock, remote wipe), a bounded OS matrix, and platform keystore / file-based encryption available.
  • A6 — Attachment storage. Server-side object storage exists or can be added for photo/signature blobs, with resumable/chunked upload support.
  • A7 — Audit is server-authoritative. The durable, tamper-evident audit history lives on the server; the client keeps only a display mirror.
  • A8 — Single offline writer per record. At most one inspector edits a given inspection offline at a time (device is assigned to one inspector); the concurrency case is inspector-offline vs supervisor-online, not two offline inspectors on the same record.
  • A9 — Bounded attachment size. ≤40 photos per inspection at a per-photo size that fits on-device encrypted storage and typical reconnect windows; exact ceilings confirmed in M0.
  • A10 — Auth can be refreshed. Existing auth issues refreshable tokens; a token can be re-obtained on reconnect before draining the queue.

If any assumption fails, the affected milestone(s) must be re-planned; A1, A3, and A4 are the highest-leverage and are treated as M0 gating decisions.

3. User flow

Before descent (online, at the surface / in the vehicle):

  1. Inspector opens the app; assigned inspections are listed (synced from server).
  2. Inspector selects one or more inspections and marks them Available offline (or the app pre-fetches assignments automatically for the shift). The inspection record, current form schema, and field values are cached; base_version is recorded. A banner confirms offline readiness.

In the basement (offline):

  1. App detects no connectivity and shows a persistent Offline — changes saved locally indicator with an unsynced-change count.
  2. Inspector opens the assigned inspection and fills form fields. Every edit is written to SQLite and appended to the outbox immediately (durable on each commit, not batched to session end).
  3. Inspector captures up to 40 photos; each is stored encrypted on disk with metadata queued for upload. A counter shows n/40. Capture beyond limits is blocked with clear feedback.
  4. Inspector collects the signature (image + capture metadata). Stored and queued like a photo.
  5. Inspector can close/reopen the app, or the device can reboot; all captured data is still present and marked unsynced.

On intermittent / restored connectivity:

  1. When signal returns (even briefly), a background sync worker drains the outbox: pushes mutations with version preconditions, uploads attachments (resumable), and pulls server changes (including any supervisor edits and the accepted status). Sync is opportunistic and resumes after drops.
  2. Conflicts, if any, are resolved by policy (§7). Overwritten inspector values are preserved in audit and surfaced for review — never silently dropped.
  3. UI transitions to Synced as items complete; partial sync is shown honestly (e.g., "12 of 40 photos uploaded").

After acceptance (post-sync):

  1. When the inspection reaches accepted, the client schedules purge of local customer data (PII rows + attachment files) for accepted_at + 24h and enforces it locally even if the device is offline at that moment (§9).

Supervisor (web, online): unchanged editing experience, but edits now participate in version-preconditioned merge with offline inspector changes and are recorded in the shared audit history.

4. Scope boundaries

In scope (pilot):

  • Offline open/read of assigned inspections.
  • Offline create/edit of form answers for one inspection type with stable field keys (the pilot form; see D7).
  • Offline capture of up to 40 photos + one signature per inspection.
  • Durable local storage, outbox, and resumable sync with version preconditions.
  • Field-level conflict merge + same-field resolution with audit preservation.
  • Server-authoritative audit history ingestion from offline mutations.
  • 24h local purge of customer data with an offline-safe backstop.
  • Encryption at rest for DB and attachment files.
  • Observability, feature flags, and a rollback path to online-only.

Out of scope (explicitly excluded):

  • Full collaborative / real-time co-editing, CRDTs, or operational transform (brief: "does not want a full collaborative editor").
  • Offline creation of brand-new inspections/assignments (A2).
  • Multi-inspector concurrent offline editing of the same record (A8).
  • Offline editing of all historical inspection types (pilot covers one).
  • Server-side re-architecture beyond the sync/attachment/audit endpoints needed here (A1 keeps this additive).
  • Cross-device offline merge for the same inspector (one device per inspector per assignment in pilot).
  • Biometric/liveness or advanced e-signature ceremony beyond captured image + metadata unless compliance requires it (D6).

5. Local data model

SQLite moves from read-through cache to offline system-of-record. New/ extended tables (names indicative):

  • inspection — id (server id), base_version (last synced server version), status, assigned_to, form_schema_version, dirty (bool), purge_deadline (nullable), last_synced_at. Form answers are stored normalized (below), not as an opaque blob, to enable field-level merge (D10).
  • inspection_answer — inspection_id, field_key, value, value_type, dirty (bool), base_version per field/section (or a dirty_fields set on the parent). Stable field_key is the merge unit.
  • attachment — attachment_id (client UUID, idempotency key), inspection_id, kind (photo | signature), local_path, content_hash, bytes, upload_state (pending | uploading | uploaded | failed), server_id (assigned after upload), created_at, mime.
  • outbox / mutation — mutation_id (client UUID), entity_type, entity_id, op (upsert | delete), field_changes (json), base_version, state (pending | inflight | conflict | done), attempts, created_at, last_error. The write path appends here transactionally with the data change.
  • audit_local — display mirror of server audit: seq, entity_id, field_key, old, new, actor, source (offline-sync | web | system), server_version, ts. Server remains authoritative (A7).
  • purge_queue — inspection_id, purge_deadline, origin (accepted | ttl-backstop), state (pending | done), receipt.
  • sync_meta — key/value: device_id, sync_cursor, schema_version, last_online_at, token_state.

Invariants:

  • Data change + outbox entry commit in the same SQLite transaction (no change without a queued mutation; no orphan mutations).
  • base_version is only advanced on confirmed server apply.
  • Every entity carries enough state to be idempotently retried (UUIDs) and to detect conflicts (versions).
  • schema_version gates migrations; downgrade is forward-only with quarantine (§13).

6. Sync protocol

Optimistic concurrency built on the server's integer record versions, with an outbox and idempotency for flaky links.

Write path (offline): each edit writes data + an outbox mutation carrying mutation_id, field_changes, and the field/record base_version the inspector started from.

Push (on connectivity): the worker sends pending mutations to a batch endpoint POST /sync (D1). Each item includes entity_id, field_changes, base_version, and mutation_id. Server behavior per item:

  • If server current_version == base_version → apply, version++, record audit, return {status: applied, new_version}.
  • If server current_version != base_version → reject with {status: conflict, server_record, current_version}.
  • If mutation_id was already applied → return {status: applied, new_version} (idempotent; safe retry).

Batch returns per-item results so a single round-trip handles many mutations — important when reconnect windows are short and volumes are high (≤40 photos + many fields).

Pull: GET /changes?since=<sync_cursor> (or per-inspection ?since=<version>) returns server-side changes — supervisor edits, status transitions (incl. accepted), and version bumps. Client applies them, updates base_version and sync_cursor.

Conflict handling: on a conflict result the client performs a three-way merge (ancestor = base_version state, ours = local edits, theirs = server record) per §7, then retries with the new base_version.

Attachments: uploaded via resumable/chunked upload keyed by attachment_id (idempotent). A photo/signature is linked to its record only after the record exists server-side (or via the batch, referencing the client UUID). Upload state advances pending → uploading → uploaded; failures are retried with Content-Range/offset resume so partial uploads survive drops.

Transport/auth: TLS; refreshable token re-obtained on reconnect before draining (A10, D9). Requests are retry-safe due to idempotency keys.

Ordering & atomicity: mutations for a record are applied in base_version order; attachment links are applied after their blob upload confirms. The worker is crash-safe: in-flight items return to pending on restart and dedupe via mutation_id.

Fallback (if A1 batch is unavailable): sequential version-preconditioned REST calls (PATCH /inspections/{id} with If-Match: <base_version>), still idempotent via mutation_id; slower over flaky links but functionally equivalent. Decided in M0/D1.

7. Conflict policy

Given "no full collaborative editor," we use field-level three-way merge with scoped ownership, not CRDTs/OT.

Ownership model (D2, D7): define which fields/sections are inspector-owned (form answers, photos, signature) vs supervisor-owned (review notes, disposition/status). Most concurrency is disjoint and merges cleanly.

Resolution rules:

  1. Disjoint fields → merge both; no conflict.
  2. Same field, both changed → server (supervisor) value wins to keep a single authoritative record, but the inspector's offline value is written to audit (overridden_value) and the inspection is flagged for review in the UI/supervisor queue. No silent loss.
  3. Delete vs update → delete wins for the record; the updated values are captured in audit before removal; if deletion is regulatory-sensitive, prefer tombstone over hard delete.
  4. Attachment collisions → attachments are additive and keyed by UUID, so they coexist; they do not overwrite each other.
  5. Status races (e.g., supervisor sets accepted while inspector still editing) → accepted is authoritative; any post-acceptance local edits are blocked at sync, surfaced to the user, and preserved in audit rather than force-applied.

Why server-wins on true conflicts: the server holds the integer version and is the concurrency arbiter (A7); supervisor edits are typically later-in-time review actions. Preserving the overridden value in audit satisfies the "audit history" regulation and keeps the model simple. This is a decision (D2) — if the business prefers inspector-wins or manual-merge-required for critical fields, that is configured per field in M0.

Guarantee: every conflict path produces an audit entry; the pilot measures conflict rate to validate A3.

8. Attachments

  • Capture: up to 40 photos + one signature per inspection. Enforce the cap at capture time with clear feedback; compress/resize to a defined max per-item size (D9/M0) to bound storage and upload time.
  • Storage: encrypted on disk (§9); metadata in attachment; binary in the app sandbox with platform file-based encryption.
  • Identity & idempotency: client-generated attachment_id (UUID) + content_hash dedupe retries and prevent duplicates over flaky links (D3).
  • Upload: resumable/chunked with offset continue; upload_state tracked; a photo is linked to the record after its blob confirms. Partial progress is shown honestly ("12/40 uploaded").
  • Ordering/failure: a failed attachment does not block text/field sync; the record can sync while attachments finish, and the inspection is marked "attachments pending" until complete.
  • Purge: attachment files and their customer metadata are deleted in the 24h purge (§9); the server retains the authoritative copies per retention rules.
  • Integrity: content_hash verified after upload; mismatch triggers re-upload.

9. Security and 24-hour purge

Encryption at rest (D4):

  • DB encrypted with SQLCipher (key in platform keystore / hardware-backed store); attachment files protected by platform file-based encryption (Android FBE / iOS Data Protection). Defense-in-depth given sensitive customer data and device-loss risk in the field. MDM enforces screen lock and offers remote wipe (A5).

Encryption in transit: TLS for all sync/upload; token-based auth with refresh (A10).

Audit history (A7): server-authoritative, append-only, tamper-evident log of every accepted mutation: actor, field, old → new, server_version, source (offline-sync vs web), and server timestamp. Overridden conflict values are logged (§7). Client keeps a display mirror only.

24-hour local purge (D5) — dual mechanism:

  1. Primary (status-driven): when sync observes accepted, set purge_deadline = accepted_at(server ts) + 24h in purge_queue. A local scheduler executes purge at/after the deadline. Purge is a local operation and needs no connectivity. It deletes customer PII rows and attachment files for that inspection, retaining only a minimal non-customer tombstone + compliance receipt ("purged at <ts>, origin accepted").
  2. Backstop (conservative TTL): because a device may stay offline and never learn the exact accepted_at (A4 risk), also auto-purge local customer data for any inspection T_backstop hours after last sync/capture, where T_backstop is chosen so the worst case still respects the 24h bound. Whichever deadline comes first triggers purge.
  3. MDM remote wipe as a last-resort enforcement for lost/never-returning devices.

Server-authoritative time (D8): purge deadlines, audit timestamps, and versions use server time; device clocks are treated as untrusted/advisory to avoid skew breaking the regulatory window.

Purge observability: every purge (and any miss) emits an event; the pilot tracks on-time purge rate as a compliance KPI.

10. Migration / backfill

  • Schema migration: bump schema_version; migrate existing read-through cache tables to the durable model (add base_version, dirty, outbox, attachment, purge, audit-mirror). Migrations run in a transaction with a pre-migration backup and are idempotent/re-runnable.
  • Backfill versions: the current cache does not track versions/dirt. On upgrade, treat all existing rows as clean and populate base_version from the server on first sync (or from cached version fields if present). No existing cached value is assumed dirty.
  • Fresh install vs upgrade: both paths tested; fresh installs create the new schema directly, upgrades migrate.
  • Form schema evolution: store form_schema_version per inspection so field keys remain stable across form changes; migrations map old→new keys where feasible.
  • Downgrade: forward-only. If a device must roll back (§13), quarantine offline data (do not delete) so a re-upgrade can resume, unless purge deadline has passed.
  • No data loss: migration acceptance requires zero loss of currently cached inspection data and correct version seeding.

11. Observability

Instrument early (wired from M2, reported via M7) so the pilot is measurable.

Metrics:

  • Sync: success/failure rate, mutations pushed/pulled per session, retry count, time-to-first-sync and time-to-full-sync after reconnect, batch latency.
  • Conflicts: rate, type (disjoint vs same-field), overrides, review-queue depth.
  • Queue: outbox depth and age, attachment upload backlog, pending/failed counts, per-inspection "attachments complete" time.
  • Offline sessions: duration, edits/photos captured offline, cache-hit rate.
  • Purge: on-time purge rate, misses, TTL-backstop triggers, receipts written.
  • Reliability: crash-free sessions, ANR/hang rate, data-loss incidents (target zero), migration success rate.

Logging: structured, sampled, privacy-safe logs (no raw customer PII in logs); correlation ids per sync session; on-device ring buffer uploadable on reconnect for support.

Dashboards/alerts: per-cohort sync health, conflict spikes, purge misses (compliance alert), upload backlog growth. Alerts wired to on-call for the pilot.

Feature-flag telemetry: which cohorts have offline enabled, kill-switch actuations, rollback events.

12. Staged rollout

Product wants a pilot before broad rollout; gates are criteria-based, not date-based.

  1. Internal / dogfood — eng + QA on managed devices in a controlled no-signal environment ( Faraday / airplane-mode drills). Exit: no data-loss incidents; sync, conflict, and purge paths verified.
  2. Pilot cohort (D7) — a small group of volunteer inspectors, one region, one inspection type, behind a feature flag. Real basements. Exit: success criteria in §1 met for a sustained period; conflict rate validates A3; purge compliance 100%; observability healthy; support runbook proven.
  3. Expanded cohorts — additional regions/inspection types in waves, each gated on the prior wave's metrics, flag-controlled, with rollback armed.
  4. General availability — offline enabled by default for eligible assignments, still flag-gated per cohort for safe throttle.

Each stage keeps the kill switch (§13) available and monitors the §11 KPIs before advancing.

13. Rollback

  • Feature-flag kill switch: disable offline capture/sync per user, cohort, or globally without an app release. On disable, the app falls back to online-only.
  • No-loss drain: before/while disabling, the app attempts to drain the outbox; if connectivity is unavailable, it preserves queued data and resumes sync when re-enabled or when signal returns — captured work is never discarded by a rollback.
  • Server-side guard: the sync endpoint can reject/queue client mutations under a server flag (e.g., if a bad client build is corrupting versions), returning a clear signal so clients pause and retry rather than lose data.
  • Schema safety: downgrade is forward-only with quarantine of offline data (§10) so a re-upgrade resumes; purge deadlines still honored during quarantine.
  • Rehearsal: rollback is exercised in the pilot with real captured data present (acceptance criterion in M8) — not assumed to work.

14. Testing

  • Unit: sync engine (push/pull, batch parsing, idempotency dedupe), three-way merge and each conflict rule (§7), outbox transactionality, migration steps, purge scheduler (accepted + TTL backstop), attachment resume/hash logic.
  • Integration: client↔server sync against a test backend exercising version preconditions and 409/conflict paths; concurrent supervisor-web edit + offline inspector edit reconciling correctly with audit preservation; attachment upload linking.
  • Network simulation / chaos: flaky links — dropped, duplicated, reordered, and delayed requests; short reconnect windows; token expiry mid-drain. Verify idempotency (no double-apply), resumable uploads, and no data loss.
  • Offline durability: process kill, app restart, device reboot, storage pressure, and low battery during capture; confirm persistence and correct unsynced-state UI.
  • Purge/compliance: on-time purge at accepted + 24h; offline-at-deadline purge; TTL backstop firing; tombstone/receipt correctness; MDM wipe path.
  • Migration: fresh install, upgrade from current cache build, downgrade + re-upgrade quarantine, form-schema-version changes.
  • Security: encryption-at-rest verification (DB + files), key storage, no-PII-in-logs checks, TLS enforcement.
  • Device/OS matrix: the managed tablet models and OS versions in scope (A5).
  • Regression guard: an automated "lost notes" scenario reproducing the original bug (disconnect after opening) as a permanent test.
  • Pilot as test: production metrics (§11) treated as acceptance evidence for rollout gates.

15. Milestone sequence (dependencies + acceptance criteria)

Sequencing only; no dates, no headcount. Complexity is qualitative (S/M/L). Parallelizable work is noted where the dependency graph allows.

M0 — Decisions & design freeze — blocking (size: S, high leverage)

  • Depends on: —
  • Blocks: all.
  • Acceptance: Every decision in §16 has an owner, chosen option, and rationale. Server sync API contract agreed (batch endpoint, version precondition, mutation_id/attachment_id idempotency, client UUIDs, accepted status, resumable upload). Field-ownership map (inspector vs supervisor) documented. Threat model + purge approach approved by security/ compliance. Attachment size/count ceilings and pilot form selected. A1/A3/A4 validated or explicitly risk-accepted.

M1 — Durable local data model & migration (size: L)

  • Depends on: M0. Blocks: M2, M3, M4, M6.
  • Acceptance: New SQLite schema (versions, dirty tracking, outbox, attachment, purge_queue, audit mirror, sync_meta) implemented; transactional data+outbox writes; migration from the current read-through cache passes for fresh install and upgrade with zero data loss and correct base_version seeding; schema_version tracked; offline edits survive restart and process kill.

M2 — Offline read & form capture, single-writer (size: M)

  • Depends on: M1. Blocks: M4. (Parallel with M3.)
  • Acceptance: With no network, inspector opens an assigned inspection, edits every in-scope field, and each edit is durably stored + queued; reopening offline shows saved state; clear offline/unsynced UI; original "disconnect after open loses notes" bug is fixed and covered by a regression test.

M3 — Offline attachments: photos + signature (size: M)

  • Depends on: M1. Blocks: M4. (Parallel with M2.)
  • Acceptance: Capture ≤40 photos + signature offline; stored encrypted with DB metadata; cap enforced with feedback; client-generated attachment_id; capture survives restart/reboot; queued for upload; signature includes capture metadata per D6.

M4 — Sync engine: push/pull with version preconditions (size: L)

  • Depends on: M2, M3. Blocks: M5, M6, M8.
  • Acceptance: On reconnect the outbox drains via the agreed sync API; mutations apply server-side with version++; pull merges server changes and accepted; idempotent retries verified under simulated flaky network (dropped/duplicated/reordered requests); resumable/chunked attachment uploads complete and hash-verify; partial progress surfaced honestly; crash-safe in-flight recovery.

M5 — Conflict resolution & audit (size: M)

  • Depends on: M4. Blocks: M9.
  • Acceptance: Concurrent supervisor-web + offline-inspector edits reconcile by field-level three-way merge; disjoint merges keep both; same-field conflicts apply the D2 policy with no silent loss (overridden value in audit + review flag); delete/update and status races handled per §7; server audit complete (actor, old→new, version, source, ts); conflict-rate telemetry emitted.

M6 — Security & 24h purge (size: M)

  • Depends on: M1, M4. Blocks: M9.
  • Acceptance: Encryption at rest (SQLCipher DB + encrypted files, keystore keys) verified; no PII in logs; TLS enforced. Purge runs on accepted within 24h using server time; offline-at-deadline purge works; conservative TTL backstop fires when accepted never observed; customer rows + attachment files deleted with tombstone/receipt retained; MDM remote-wipe path tested; purge compliance measurable.

M7 — Observability & feature flags (size: M, cross-cutting)

  • Depends on: M2 (instrumentation), integrated through M4–M6. Blocks: M9 (rollout gates need metrics), M8 (flags).
  • Acceptance: §11 metrics, structured privacy-safe logs, dashboards, and alerts live; feature flags gate offline capture/sync per user/cohort; global kill switch functional; flag telemetry present.

M8 — Rollback mechanism (size: S/M)

  • Depends on: M7 (flags), M4. Blocks: M9.
  • Acceptance: Disabling offline falls back to online-only without losing captured/unsynced data (drain-or-preserve verified); server-side guard can pause client sync; schema downgrade quarantines offline data and re-upgrade resumes; rollback rehearsed with real data present.

M9 — Pilot (size: M)

  • Depends on: M2, M3, M4, M5, M6, M7, M8. Blocks: M10.
  • Acceptance: Limited cohort/region/form behind flag in real no-signal use; §1 success criteria met for the defined pilot duration; conflict rate validates A3; 100% on-time purge; rollback available and unexercised-or-successful; support runbook + feedback loop in place; exit criteria reviewed and signed off.

M10 — Broad rollout (size: M)

  • Depends on: M9 exit criteria met. Blocks: —
  • Acceptance: Wave-based cohort expansion gated on §11 KPIs; offline enabled by default for eligible assignments (still flag-throttled); documentation, on-call, and rollback readiness confirmed for each wave.

Critical path: M0 → M1 → {M2 ∥ M3} → M4 → M5 → M9 → M10, with M6, M7, M8 joining before M9. M7 instrumentation should begin alongside M2 to avoid a late observability crunch.

16. Decisions required before implementation (with recommendations)

Each must be resolved in M0. Recommendation given; owner to confirm.

  • D1 — Sync API shape: batch POST /sync vs sequential REST. Recommend: batch endpoint with per-item base_version + mutation_id idempotency; sequential version-preconditioned PATCH (If-Match) as fallback if the server cannot add batch. Why: short reconnect windows + high mutation volume (≤40 photos + fields) make round-trips expensive; batch + idempotency is robust to retries. (Validates A1.)

  • D2 — Conflict granularity & winner. Recommend: field-level three-way merge with scoped ownership; on true same-field conflict, server/supervisor wins, inspector value preserved in audit + review flag. Why: honors "no collaborative editor," keeps a single authoritative record, and satisfies the audit regulation with no silent loss. Per-field override (inspector-wins / manual-required) configurable for critical fields. (Validates A3.)

  • D3 — Identity for offline-created sub-records. Recommend: client-generated UUIDs for attachments and offline-created answer/attachment rows as idempotency keys; server maps UUID→integer id on first apply. Inspections remain server-assigned (A2). Why: enables offline creation + idempotent retries without id collisions.

  • D4 — Encryption at rest. Recommend: SQLCipher for the DB + platform file-based encryption for attachments, keys in hardware-backed keystore, MDM lock/wipe. Why: defense-in-depth for sensitive customer data and field device-loss risk; supports regulatory posture. (Validates A5.)

  • D5 — Purge trigger & offline enforcement. Recommend: primary status-driven purge at accepted_at + 24h (server time), plus a conservative local TTL backstop, plus MDM wipe; purge is local (needs no connectivity); retain tombstone/receipt. Why: guarantees the 24h bound even if a device never re-syncs after acceptance. (Validates A4; risk in RESPONSE.md.)

  • D6 — Signature capture & legal validity. Recommend: on-device signature image + capture metadata (timestamp, signer name, optional geo) submitted as an attachment; confirm legal sufficiency with compliance (whether additional ceremony/attestation is required). Why: signature is a named requirement; validity rules must be fixed before build.

  • D7 — Pilot scope (form / fields / region / cohort). Recommend: one high-value inspection type with stable field keys and disjoint inspector/supervisor ownership; one region; small volunteer cohort. Why: bounds conflict complexity and tests the riskiest assumptions (A1/A3) first.

  • D8 — Clock-skew handling. Recommend: server-authoritative timestamps for audit, versions, and purge deadlines; device clocks advisory only. Why: unreliable device time must not break the regulatory window or version ordering.

  • D9 — Attachment size/compression ceilings & transport. Recommend: define max per-photo size with on-device compression, resumable chunked uploads, and content_hash verification; reuse existing auth with refresh-on-reconnect. Why: bounds storage/upload time within short reconnect windows and keeps retries safe. (Validates A6/A9.)

  • D10 — Form data representation. Recommend: normalize answers keyed by stable field_key (not opaque blobs), versioned by form_schema_version. Why: prerequisite for field-level merge (D2) and for evolving forms without breaking sync/merge.

17. Open risks carried into M0

Tracked here and summarized in RESPONSE.md: A1 (server extensibility), A3 (field-level mergeability / disjoint ownership), and A4/D5 (guaranteeing the 24h purge on devices that stay offline). These are the three riskiest assumptions and gate the design; each has a mitigation and a validation point in M0/pilot.

qwen3.8-max/06-product-planning/TASK.md

Task 06 — Product and engineering planning: offline inspection sync

Create PLAN.md for adding offline work to a tablet-based building inspection app. Use BRIEF.md as the only product input.

The plan should make assumptions explicit and cover user flow, scope boundaries, local data model, sync protocol, conflict policy, attachments, security, migration/backfill, observability, staged rollout, rollback, and testing. Include a milestone sequence with dependencies and acceptance criteria. Identify the decisions that must be made before implementation and offer a recommendation for each. Avoid fake dates and unjustified staffing estimates.

Write RESPONSE.md summarizing the three riskiest assumptions. Work only in this directory.

Evaluation 7 / 10 graded blind as submission S

A reasonable mid-tier plan. It uses row-per-question merge with a 409 review screen for same-field edits, priority push classes, chunked uploads and an M0 decision gate. The purge recommendation (D1) is to purge at observed acceptance + 24h, backed by a daily check-in policy. That can leave data well past the regulatory window, and the plan relies on compliance accepting it. The milestone ACs are partly thin, and audit events are pushed separately from data.

Strengths

  • D3: 409 plus human review screen, with the LWW-by-clock rejection reasoned
  • D6 priority classes so form data is not starved behind photos
  • M0 'Blocks everything'; dependency-ordered M1-M10

Weaknesses

  • The purge timer starts at local observation and fires 24h later, so data could persist up to 24h plus the offline gap past acceptance
  • Audit events are pushed as separate ops ahead of answers, which risks a mismatch between audit and data
  • 'Files are overwritten' on flash is naive; the pilot runs 'multiple weeks' without coverage criteria
Evidence the grader checked
  • S/PLAN.md:209-216 purge; :380 D1
  • S/PLAN.md:145-150 push priority
  • S/PLAN.md:333-371 milestones
  • S/RESPONSE.md: purge interpretation, conflict rarity and photo sync

Objective checks

Files

glm-5.3/06-product-planning/RESPONSE.md

Response: three riskiest assumptions

1. The 24-hour purge is satisfiable by purging when the device observes acceptance (A7 / D1). The regulation is written against wall-clock time after acceptance, but a tablet in a basement cannot know an inspection was accepted, and no engineering can force a device online. Our plan bets that compliance accepts "purge within 24h of local observation + fleet monitoring for dark devices." If they instead require the clock to start at server acceptance, we need forced-sync policies, cryptographic remote delete, or MDM-level wipes — a materially different and more expensive design. This must be settled at M0 before any implementation.

2. Conflicts are rare and a human review screen is enough (A3/A4). The whole conflict design (409 + merge review, no collaborative editing, no timestamp last-writer-wins) depends on supervisor/web edits overlapping field sessions only occasionally. If concurrency turns out to be routine, inspectors and supervisors will hit the review screen constantly, the pilot's "no support tickets" criterion will fail, and we will be forced toward heavier merge machinery that product explicitly does not want. The pilot's measured 409-rate and merge-review completion metrics are the earliest real signal; we should instrument conflict rate from the first dogfood build.

3. 40 photos per inspection can actually be synced over intermittent, seconds-long connectivity windows (A5/A6), and devices check in at least daily (A10). A full inspection is ~100–300 MB; chunked resumable upload makes this tractable, but the bet still requires that field devices reliably regain some connectivity every working day and that the backend tolerates hundreds of long-running resumable uploads at pilot scale. If real basements yield even less bandwidth or devices go dark for days, sync backlogs compound, the "fully synced within one working day" pilot criterion fails, and — worse — the purge obligation in assumption 1 gets harder because the device that most needs to sync is the one that never does.

All three risks are addressed in PLAN.md §14 as decisions D1, D3/D4, and D5, each with a recommendation and an explicit point at which the assumption gets tested.

glm-5.3/06-product-planning/BRIEF.md

Offline inspection brief

Inspectors use company-managed tablets in basements with no signal. Today, a lost connection after opening an inspection can discard notes. They need to open assigned inspections, fill forms, take up to 40 photos, and collect a signature offline. Connectivity may return intermittently. Supervisors can edit the same inspection from the web. Regulations require an audit history and removal of local customer data within 24 hours after an inspection is accepted. Existing server APIs use REST with integer record versions. The mobile app has SQLite but currently treats it as a read-through cache. Product wants a pilot before broad rollout and does not want a full collaborative editor.

glm-5.3/06-product-planning/PLAN.md

Plan: Offline Inspection Sync

Input: BRIEF.md only. No dates or staffing estimates are given; work is sequenced as milestones with dependencies instead. Every assumption is stated explicitly so it can be challenged before implementation.

1. Assumptions (explicit)

These are assumptions, not facts. Each is revisited in the "Open decisions" section where a recommendation is made.

  • A1 — Platform. "Company-managed tablets" means a managed fleet (MDM-enrolled) running a known, recent OS version. The app is native and can access local storage, secure keystore, and background OS facilities.
  • A2 — Server extensibility. The existing REST API can gain new endpoints (batch/delta pull, patch push, resumable attachment upload) without breaking existing web clients. Integer record versions already give us optimistic concurrency control per record.
  • A3 — Single field editor. An inspection is worked in the field by exactly one inspector at a time; concurrency comes only from supervisors editing from the web. Inspectors do not edit each other's inspections.
  • A4 — Conflict rarity. Supervisor/web edits during an active field session are the exception, not the norm. Conflicts will be rare enough that a merge-review screen (not a collaborative editor) is acceptable. Product has explicitly ruled out a full collaborative editor.
  • A5 — Attachment budget. "Up to 40 photos" per inspection; assuming ~3–8 MB per compressed photo, an inspection's attachments total roughly 100–300 MB. Signature is a small image/PDF.
  • A6 — Connectivity pattern. Offline stretches of hours (basement), then short, possibly weak connectivity windows. Sync must make progress in windows measured in seconds and must tolerate mid-transfer drops.
  • A7 — Compliance interpretation. "Removal of local customer data within 24 hours after acceptance" is satisfiable by purging on the device when the acceptance event is observed locally, backed by fleet-level monitoring. This is a legal interpretation and must be confirmed with compliance (see D1).
  • A8 — Audit semantics. Every field change, photo capture, signature capture, and state transition must produce an immutable audit event that eventually reaches the server; local audit events are as binding as server ones until synced.
  • A9 — Forms are versioned. A form definition is frozen per inspection at assignment/checkout; the server does not mutate a form definition under an in-progress inspection.
  • A10 — Device check-in expectation. Fleet policy can require devices to reach the network at least once per working day (charging station, vehicle, office). This bounds how stale a device and how late a purge can be.

2. User flow (field inspector)

  1. Pre-departure (online). Inspector opens the app; assigned inspections ("work package": inspection records + frozen form definitions + customer context + prior attachments metadata) sync down and are marked available offline. UI shows a clear "Ready for offline" state per inspection, including attachment completeness.
  2. In the basement (offline). Inspector opens an assigned inspection, fills forms, takes up to 40 photos, collects the signature. Everything is written to the local store first (local is the system of record while offline). Nothing can be lost on connection drop — the current "lost connection discards notes" failure mode is eliminated by construction because writes never depend on the network.
  3. Connectivity returns (intermittent). Sync runs opportunistically in the background: audit events and form edits push first (small, high value), then attachments upload with resume. Progress is visible in a sync status screen. If a supervisor edited the same inspection, a conflict review screen appears (see §6).
  4. Acceptance. Inspection is marked complete/accepted (by supervisor on web, per current process). Once the acceptance event is observed on the tablet, a 24-hour purge timer starts locally; customer data and attachments are deleted and the deletion is itself audit-logged and reported.

Supervisor web flow is unchanged except: (a) a soft indicator when an inspection is checked out offline, and (b) the conflict/merge behavior in §6.

3. Scope boundaries

In scope

  • Offline open/read of assigned inspections, form fill, photo capture (≤40), signature capture.
  • Two-way sync of structured edits and attachments for assigned inspections.
  • Conflict detection and a review UI (not collaborative editing).
  • Audit history for all local mutations; local purge after acceptance.
  • Pilot for a limited inspector cohort with a kill switch.

Out of scope (explicitly)

  • Real-time collaborative editing or presence (ruled out by product).
  • Offline access to anything beyond the inspector's assigned work package (the store stays a bounded cache for everything else).
  • Editing inspections not assigned to the signed-in inspector.
  • New backend platform work beyond new REST endpoints; no event bus, no CRDT infrastructure.
  • Offline user administration, reassignment, or scheduling flows.
  • Push notifications / server-initiated commands to offline devices (a device only learns about server changes when it pulls).

4. Local data model

SQLite stops being a read-through cache and becomes a first-class store for assigned inspections, with the server still the ultimate system of record.

Tables (logical):

  • inspection — server fields + local_state (synced / dirty / conflicted), base_version (integer server version per record, used for optimistic concurrency), form_version (frozen definition).
  • form_answer — one row per question: inspection_id, question_id, value, base_version, dirty. Row-per-question is what makes field-level merge possible without diffing opaque blobs.
  • attachment — client_uuid, inspection_id, kind (photo | signature), content_hash (SHA-256), bytes, capture_ts, upload_state (pending / uploading / uploaded / failed), uploaded_chunks.
  • audit_event — append-only: client_uuid, inspection_id, entity, entity_id, mutation, payload_digest, client_ts, synced flag. Never updated, never compacted locally.
  • outbox — ordered pending operations with idempotency_key (client UUID), type, payload, attempts, next_attempt_at. All pushes flow through it; the audit log records what happened, the outbox records what must still be sent (they are not the same thing).
  • meta — schema version, last-pull cursors per record type, device install id.

Attachment bytes: photos live as files in app-private storage with the row above as metadata; the content_hash plus bytes lets the server dedupe. Rationale in D2. Signature is stored the same way but is immutable after capture (any correction is a new signature plus a supersede audit event).

Migration/backfill of the existing cache (§9) is a schema-version bump that (1) creates the new tables, (2) keeps existing cached read-only data only if it is still needed for the work package, and (3) never fabricates base_version values — a record gets a real version only after a pull.

5. Sync protocol

Pattern: pull-delta + push-outbox, both batched, both idempotent, both resumable. Server remains authoritative; the client never trusts its own clock for ordering.

Pull. Per record type, "give me everything changed since cursor" (cursor = max integer version seen for that type, per assignment scope). Pull runs before push at each sync attempt so the client rebases on fresh state. Server returns records with versions and soft-deletes/tombstones. Response is chunked so a weak link can complete a pull in several windows.

Push. Outbox drains oldest-first within a priority order: audit events → form answers → attachment metadata → attachment bytes. Each operation carries a client-generated idempotency key; the server keeps a short idempotency cache so replayed operations after a dropped response are safe. Form-answer pushes carry base_version; the server either applies (returning the new version) or returns 409 with the current server record (see §6).

Attachments. Chunked, resumable upload over REST: init (hash, size, kind) → upload chunks by index with byte-range verification → commit. Chunks are small enough (order 256 KB–1 MB) that a few seconds of connectivity makes progress. Downloads of pre-existing attachments use plain HTTP range requests into the same store. Hash-based dedupe on both sides.

Cadence. Sync triggers: app foreground, connectivity change, periodic backoff while dirty data exists, manual "Sync now". Everything is safe to kill mid-flight; SQLite commits are transactional per operation batch and chunk uploads are individually acknowledged.

Clocks. Client timestamps are advisory metadata only. Ordering and conflict detection use server-assigned versions; audit events are ordered by (client sequence, server receipt). Devices with badly skewed clocks must not be able to affect any decision.

6. Conflict policy

Two sources of concurrency: supervisor (web) vs inspector (tablet), because A3 rules out inspector-vs-inspector.

  • Different fields: merge cleanly. Row-per-question answers + integer versions make this a non-event; both sides' writes apply.
  • Same field, both changed since the common base: server rejects the tablet's push with 409 + current server value. Client marks the answer conflicted, keeps both values (local + server), and shows a review screen when the inspector next opens the inspection. The reviewer picks one value or re-enters it; the resolution is itself an audit event.
  • Structural conflicts (inspection accepted on web while tablet still edits): acceptance wins. Tablet moves to read-only with a clear message; unpushed edits are preserved in the audit log and surfaced to the supervisor rather than silently dropped.
  • Attachments never conflict. Photos/signatures are append-only (client UUID identity), so concurrent capture is impossible by construction.
  • No last-writer-wins by timestamp, no automatic same-field overwrite. Same-field collisions always surface to a human. This is the "no collaborative editor" line: we detect and review, we don't merge prose.

Supervisor side: when an inspection is checked out, the web shows "being edited in the field" as a soft warning (no hard lock — see D5).

7. Security

  • At rest. Structured data in SQLCipher (or platform equivalent) with the key in the hardware-backed keystore/keychain; photo files in app-private storage relying on OS per-app file-based encryption, with keys non-exportable and unusable on a different device. No customer data in shared storage, logs, analytics, or screenshots-able cache locations.
  • In transit. TLS only, certificate pinning optional (decide with security team), no new crypto of our own.
  • Auth. Existing session mechanism; offline sessions use a locally stored token/refresh material per current app policy — flag if tokens expire faster than a field day (see D7). No offline auth bypass; the work package is scoped to the signed-in inspector.
  • Device loss. MDM remote wipe + the 24h purge (§8) bound exposure. A device reported lost gets its sessions revoked server-side; work-package pull tokens can be scoped per assignment so revocation is fast.
  • 24-hour purge. When acceptance is observed locally (via pull), schedule purge of that inspection's customer data and attachments at acceptance_observed_ts + 24h (or earlier at next sync after 24h from server-acceptance — see D1). The purge: deletes rows + files, writes a local_purge audit event, reports purge completion to the server so compliance can see devices that are overdue. Nothing is ever "hidden but recoverable" — files are overwritten/deleted, not merely unlinked where the OS allows.
  • Signature integrity. Signature image + capture timestamp + inspector identity are hash-chained into the audit event so tampering is detectable.

8. Migration / backfill

  • Server. New endpoints are additive (delta pull, outbox apply, chunked attachment upload, purge report). Integer-version machinery is reused everywhere; existing web clients are untouched. Server must add: idempotency cache, per-inspection attachment manifest, form-definition versioning if not already present (A9).
  • Client schema migration. Bump SQLite schema version; create new tables; do not attempt to "upgrade" cached rows into versioned editable rows — old cache content is discarded and replaced by the first full pull. This avoids fabricating versions and keeps the migration trivial to reason about.
  • Backfill. No server backfill of historical data is needed: offline capture only applies to newly assigned inspections. Existing inspections in flight at rollout simply stay online-only until they complete.
  • Form freeze. At rollout, ensure assignment time snapshots the current form definition version so A9 holds; if the server doesn't support this today, it is a server prerequisite (M1 dependency), not a client concern.

9. Observability

Client (batched, uploaded with sync, never blocking it):

  • Sync outcomes per attempt (pull ok/fail, push ok/fail/409), queue depths by type, oldest unsent item age ("data staleness").
  • Attachment upload progress distribution: chunk retries, throughput, time to fully sync an inspection after capture.
  • Conflict rate: fraction of pushed answers that 409, per inspection.
  • Purge: acceptance-observed → purge-completed latency distribution and count of overdue purges (the compliance SLA metric).
  • Offline session length, storage usage, migration success, crash reports.

Server:

  • Idempotency-cache hit rate (replay storms indicate flaky links).
  • Delta-pull and chunk-upload success rates and latency; per-device last-seen to detect dark devices (feeds D1 risk).
  • 409 rate and merge-review completion rate (tells us if A4 is wrong).

Dashboards exist before the pilot (M6), because the pilot's go/no-go depends on these numbers.

10. Staged rollout

  1. Internal dogfood. Engineering + friendly supervisors with synthetic and real assignments; airplane-mode drills are part of normal testing.
  2. Pilot cohort. One region/team of inspectors, chosen to include the worst basements. Explicit success criteria (below) evaluated over multiple weeks of real work.
  3. Staged broad rollout. Percentage/ring-based by team, each ring gated on the same metrics with no regression.
  4. Kill switch. A server-delivered flag disables offline capture and reverts the app to the current online-only behavior (store back to read-through semantics). The flag must be honored at app start and at sync time.

Pilot success criteria (acceptance gate to broad rollout):

  • Zero data-loss reports of field-captured content (the current bug class).
  • ≥99% of inspections fully synced (including all attachments) within one working day of capture, with the long tail understood.
  • Conflict rate consistent with A4 (a few percent of inspections at most); all conflicts resolved through the review UI without support tickets.
  • 100% of accepted inspections purged locally within 24h of observed acceptance, with zero compliance findings.
  • Crash-free session rate not worse than the online-only baseline.

11. Rollback

  • Client. Kill-switch flag returns the app to online-only; pending outbox content is either flushed first (preferred) or preserved on device until data can be recovered — never silently deleted by a rollback. The new schema must be tolerated by the old code path (additive tables, cache tables still populated for read-through).
  • Server. Additive endpoints can be disabled by flag; old clients never call them. Disabling outbox-apply strands pending client data, so server rollback pairs with the client kill switch and a comms plan, and uses the same outbox-drain-first rule.
  • Data. The purge is the only destructive client operation; it has its own safeguard (audit event + server acknowledgment) and is excluded from rollback paths. Server data written by sync is normal audited data; no special rollback needed beyond standard correction flows.

12. Testing

  • Sync engine unit tests (deterministic, simulated transport): drop, delay, duplicate, and reorder every message; idempotency-key replays; cursor rollback; kill mid-batch at every boundary. Property/fuzz tests on outbox ordering and priority.
  • Conflict tests (table-driven): matrix of {web-only, tablet-only, both, same-field, different-field, accept-races-edit} — assert exact final state and audit content.
  • Clock-skew tests: devices with skewed clocks cannot win conflicts or corrupt audit ordering.
  • Attachment tests: 40-photo inspections over simulated intermittent links; resume after kill at every chunk boundary; dedupe by hash; low-disk and corrupted-file handling.
  • Purge tests: timer firing, purge idempotency, overdue-purge alerting, verification that files (not just rows) are gone; purge runs even if the device never syncs again until reconnect.
  • Migration tests: upgrade from the shipping cache schema from every recent released version; fresh-install path.
  • Audit correctness tests: audit log is append-only under adversarial sequences; every mutation produces exactly one event; signature hash chain verifies.
  • End-to-end/field tests: scripted airplane-mode drill (open → fill → 40 photos → signature → offline accept race → reconnect); real basement days during dogfood and pilot.
  • Server tests: idempotency cache under replay; delta pull correctness across concurrent version assignment; load test of chunked upload at pilot cohort scale.

13. Milestones (ordered by dependency; no dates)

  • M0 — Decisions locked. D1–D8 (below) answered and written down; compliance sign-off on the purge interpretation (D1) and security sign-off on §7. Blocks everything.
  • M1 — Server prerequisites. Delta-pull endpoints with per-type cursors; form-definition freeze at assignment; idempotency cache design; attachment manifest. Depends on M0. AC: web client unaffected; delta pull returns correct changes incl. tombstones; form version frozen per assignment.
  • M2 — Local store foundation. New SQLite schema, migration from shipping cache, encryption at rest, append-only audit log, work-package pull (online only, no offline editing yet). Depends on M1. AC: upgrade from shipping app version works; work package fully browsable after airplane mode; audit events recorded for reads-by-assignment and pushes; zero fabricated versions.
  • M3 — Offline capture. Forms, photos, signature fully offline via local writes; the old "connection loss discards notes" path is removed. Depends on M2. AC: airplane-mode end-to-end capture drill passes; kill the app at any point with no loss; 40-photo inspection stored within device budget.
  • M4 — Sync engine. Outbox push, 409 handling, chunked resumable attachment upload, sync status UI. Depends on M3 (and M1 endpoints). AC: intermittent-link simulation fully drains an inspection including 40 photos; idempotent replays safe; crash at any boundary resumes.
  • M5 — Conflicts & supervisor concurrency. Conflict review UI, web "being edited in the field" indicator, accept-races-edit handling. Depends on M4. AC: conflict matrix tests pass end-to-end against real web edits; no silent drops; resolution audit-logged.
  • M6 — Compliance & purge. 24h purge timer, purge acknowledgment, overdue-purge alerting. Depends on M4 (acceptance arrives via pull). AC: purge tests pass; compliance demonstrates the flow on a real device.
  • M7 — Observability & flags. Client telemetry, dashboards, kill switch. Depends on M4 (metrics ride on sync). AC: dashboards live for all §9 metrics; kill switch verified to revert a pilot build.
  • M8 — Dogfood. Internal field use including real basements. Depends on M5–M7. AC: no data loss; drill checklist executed; conflict and purge metrics collected.
  • M9 — Pilot. External cohort under the §10 criteria. Depends on M8. AC: all five pilot success criteria met; go/no-go review documented.
  • M10 — Broad rollout. Ring-based rollout, each ring gated on unchanged metrics. Depends on M9.

Rollback readiness (verified kill switch + drain-first rule) is an entry criterion for M9, not an afterthought.

14. Open decisions (must be made before implementation)

# Decision Options Recommendation
D1 When does the 24h purge clock start, and what happens if the device is offline past the deadline? (a) server-acceptance time, device must be forced online; (b) local observation of acceptance; (c) hybrid (b) + monitoring: purge at observed + 24h, plus per-device last-seen alerting and a fleet policy requiring daily check-in (A10). Forcing devices online (a) is operationally unrealistic in basements; but get compliance to confirm (b) satisfies the regulation — this is a legal question, not an engineering one.
D2 Photo bytes: SQLite blobs vs files+metadata (a) blobs in DB; (b) files in app-private storage, metadata in SQLite (b): 40 photos ≈ 100–300 MB would bloat the DB and WAL, slow commits, and make encrypted backups clumsy; per-file OS encryption (hardware-backed) is simpler and streaming-friendly. Trade-off (two stores to keep transactionally consistent) is manageable with the content-hash as the join key and orphan sweeps.
D3 Same-field conflict resolution (a) last-writer-wins by timestamp; (b) server 409 + human review screen; (c) field-level 3-way auto-merge (b): matches "no collaborative editor", keeps humans accountable for audit-relevant answers, and is far cheaper than (c). LWW-by-clock (a) is unacceptable for regulated data given skew.
D4 Should supervisor web edits be blocked while an inspection is checked out? (a) hard lock; (b) soft indicator only; (c) nothing (b): hard locks create deadlocks when a tablet is lost/broken; doing nothing invites avoidable conflicts. The soft indicator plus D3 review covers the residual risk.
D5 Attachment upload transport (a) plain multipart retries; (b) chunked resumable REST upload (tus-like) (b): with seconds-long connectivity windows, (a) restarts 100 MB uploads on every drop and the pilot will drown in failed syncs. (b) costs one server endpoint and pays for itself in the first basement.
D6 Push ordering guarantee (a) strict per-inspection FIFO; (b) priority classes (audit → answers → attachments) (b) with FIFO within a class: audit events and answers are tiny and must never be starved behind 300 MB of photos; attachments are idempotent and resumable so reordering them is harmless.
D7 Offline session/token lifetime extend token TTL vs local re-auth material Depends on current auth design (unknown from brief). Recommendation: verify a session survives a full offline field day; if tokens expire sooner, add a renewable offline credential scoped to the work package rather than extending global token TTL. Needs security sign-off at M0.
D8 Pilot device scope whole fleet vs newest subset Newest-hardware subset for the pilot: encryption-at-rest guarantees (D2) and storage budgets are safest there; expand rings only after metrics hold.

15. Risks not covered elsewhere

  • Regulatory: D1 is the largest compliance risk; if compliance insists on server-time deadlines, we need forced-sync or cryptographic remote-delete designs, which change scope materially.
  • Storage: worst case (40 photos × many inspections per day) needs a device storage budget and an eviction policy for uploaded attachments — evict-after-upload must not violate the audit requirement (audit events remain; bytes can go once the server has acknowledged them).
  • Flaky-clock devices corrupting ordering — mitigated by server-version authority (§5) and tested explicitly (§12).

glm-5.3/06-product-planning/TASK.md

Task 06 — Product and engineering planning: offline inspection sync

Create PLAN.md for adding offline work to a tablet-based building inspection app. Use BRIEF.md as the only product input.

The plan should make assumptions explicit and cover user flow, scope boundaries, local data model, sync protocol, conflict policy, attachments, security, migration/backfill, observability, staged rollout, rollback, and testing. Include a milestone sequence with dependencies and acceptance criteria. Identify the decisions that must be made before implementation and offer a recommendation for each. Avoid fake dates and unjustified staffing estimates.

Write RESPONSE.md summarizing the three riskiest assumptions. Work only in this directory.

Evaluation 6.5 / 10 graded blind as submission K

Covers all sections with tidy structure, decisions with options, and M0-M10 with dependencies. But the purge mechanics are thin (Q3 even asks whether the clock is server or device time). Encryption at rest defaults to OS-only for regulated PII. Every version mismatch forces explicit per-field resolution even for non-overlapping edits. Rollback relies on binary downgrade, which leaves 'ghost rows'. Many invented numbers (≤25 inspectors, ≥90%, 10x load, TTL-30min).

Strengths

  • Envelope plus idempotency-key design with 409/412/429 handling
  • Stage exit criteria are measurable; RESPONSE explains why it chose its three risks

Weaknesses

  • D1 recommends OS-only encryption for v1
  • D2(A): explicit per-field resolution for every conflict, including non-overlapping fields; the enum LWW rule is confused
  • Rollback: 'Tablets re-downgrade to the previous build' and offline records 'become ghost rows', which strands queued data
  • RESPONSE proposes relaxing the purge rule to '24h after the device next comes online', which is legally doubtful
Evidence the grader checked

  • K/PLAN.md:362-368 rollback table
